LLM Quantization

The precision you remove, the error you create, and the speed you actually get.

Mathematical derivations and worked exercises

Each derivation states its assumptions, shows the intermediate steps, and explains what follows. Try each exercise before opening its worked solution.

§How to use this document

This guide extends the LLM Inference Systems guide's short quantization chapter. The emphasis here is the numerical mechanism and the path from a compressed checkpoint to a measured deployment. It assumes you know that a transformer has linear projections, attention, a prefill phase, and autoregressive decode; Appendix B defines the rest.

  • First pass: §0–§2 and the interactive lab. Be able to calculate a quantized value and explain how one outlier changes the scale.
  • Second pass: §3–§5. Separate the algorithms that choose quantized values from the formats that store them, and treat weights, activations, and KV cache independently.
  • Third pass: §6–§9. Calculate memory, predict the likely bottleneck, and read the evidence tables before designing an evaluation on your own workload.
The thesis, up front

A bit width is only the start of a quantization design. What is quantized, where scales live, how outliers are handled, and which kernel consumes the packed representation determine both model quality and speed. A 4-bit checkpoint can save memory yet run slower; a nominally larger 8-bit format can win at large batch sizes if it reaches efficient low-precision matrix multiplication.

0The mental model

Quantization replaces many possible numeric values with a smaller set of representable values. Its three benefits must be measured separately: storage, memory traffic, and arithmetic.

0.1 Three targets, three lifetimes

TargetWhen createdMain savingMain difficulty
Weights WWWTraining; static at inferenceCheckpoint size and HBM weight readsSmall errors accumulate across layers; important columns differ.
Activations XXXEvery forward passLow-precision GEMM and some activation trafficInput-dependent ranges and rare, large channels.
KV cache K,VK,VK,VEvery token; retained for the sequenceContext capacity, batch size, and attention readsErrors can change attention scores across long contexts.

Gradients and optimizer states can also be quantized during training, but that is a separate optimization problem. This guide concentrates on inference and includes QLoRA only to clarify why its 4-bit training representation is not automatically a fast 4-bit serving representation.

0.2 Compression is not a speedup

Take a linear layer Y=XWY = XWY=XW. In a weight-only W4A16 path, stored weights use roughly four bits each, but the runtime may unpack them, multiply by scales, and then use 16-bit arithmetic. A fused kernel can exploit fewer HBM bytes during small-batch decode; a poor kernel can erase the gain with unpacking and launch overhead. To use INT8 or FP8 tensor-core arithmetic on the matrix multiply, the activation operand must have a compatible low-precision representation too. Hardware and implementation matter as much as the quantizer. GPTQ's original paper explicitly notes this distinction. [2]

Tend−to−end≈Tweight traffic+TKV traffic+Tmatrix+Tdequant/requant+Tnon ⁣- ⁣GEMM+Tscheduling.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{end-to-end}}\approx{}&T_{\mathrm{weight\ traffic}}+T_{\mathrm{KV\ traffic}}+T_{\mathrm{matrix}}\\&+T_{\mathrm{dequant/requant}}+T_{\mathrm{non\!\text{-}\!GEMM}}+T_{\mathrm{scheduling}}.\end{aligned}Tend−to−end​≈​Tweight traffic​+TKV traffic​+Tmatrix​+Tdequant/requant​+Tnon-GEMM​+Tscheduling​.​

Quantization changes some terms, not all. In prefill, large matrix multiplies often make arithmetic throughput important. At batch-one decode, repeatedly reading weights often makes bandwidth dominant. With long contexts or high concurrency, KV reads and cache capacity can dominate instead. These are workload-dependent regimes, not universal labels. [15]

0.3 Define the optimization problem before choosing a method

A quantizer is successful when it changes a deployment constraint without unacceptable behavior loss. For a fixed pretrained model, formulate a constrained problem: minimize inference cost C(recipe,kernel,workload)C(\mathrm{recipe},\mathrm{kernel},\mathrm{workload})C(recipe,kernel,workload) subject to task loss increase at most ε\varepsilon ε, peak memory at most MMM, and an inter-token latency target. For training, the objective instead includes convergence over a token budget and total training cost. A compressed checkpoint is an intermediate artifact in either problem.

The research literature optimizes several proxies for this objective. RTN minimizes local rounding distance; GPTQ uses calibration-weighted output error; AWQ redistributes channel resolution; OmniQuant reconstructs blocks; rotation methods change the quantization basis; QAT changes trainable parameters under a quantized forward model. None of these proxies is identical to the user's final task. The practical skill is to understand why a proxy helps, where it fails, and what its runtime can exploit.

Two distinctions organize this guide. Error geometry: which values/directions matter, and which errors can cancel? Execution geometry: which values share a scale, tile, kernel, memory transaction, or device? A numerical transform that ignores execution geometry may be too expensive. A hardware-friendly grid that ignores error geometry may ruin a sensitive layer. The best recipe satisfies both.

1The arithmetic, from one number to a model

1.1 Scale, zero point, rounding, clipping

For an affine bbb-bit integer quantizer, choose a real scale s>0s > 0s>0, integer zero point zzz, and integer range [qmin⁡,qmax⁡][q_{\min},q_{\max}][qmin​,qmax​]. Quantization stores an integer; dequantization maps it back to an approximation:

q=clip⁡ ⁣(round⁡ ⁣(xs)+z,  qmin⁡,qmax⁡),x^=s(q−z),e=x^−x.\begin{aligned}q&=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac xs\right)+z,\;q_{\min},q_{\max}\right),\\\widehat x&=s(q-z),\\e&=\widehat x-x.\end{aligned}qxe​=clip(round(sx​)+z,qmin​,qmax​),=s(q−z),=x−x.​

For symmetric signed quantization, use z=0z = 0z=0, qmax⁡=2b−1−1q_{\max}=2^{b-1}-1qmax​=2b−1−1, and often qmin⁡=−qmax⁡q_{\min}=-q_{\max}qmin​=−qmax​; the unused most-negative code keeps positive and negative coverage symmetric. For an affine mapping fitted to observed [xmin⁡,xmax⁡][x_{\min},x_{\max}][xmin​,xmax​], a common choice is s=xmax⁡−xmin⁡qmax⁡−qmin⁡s=\frac{x_{\max}-x_{\min}}{q_{\max}-q_{\min}}s=qmax​−qmin​xmax​−xmin​​ and z=round⁡(qmin⁡−xmin⁡/s)z=\operatorname{round}(q_{\min}-x_{\min}/s)z=round(qmin​−xmin​/s), clipped to the integer range. Rounding conventions and endpoints vary by library, so the actual format specification is authoritative.

Worked value: four-bit symmetric integers have qmax⁡=7q_{\max}=7qmax​=7. If a group's largest magnitude is 1.41.41.4, then s=0.2s = 0.2s=0.2. A weight 0.530.530.53 becomes q=round⁡(2.65)=3q=\operatorname{round}(2.65)=3q=round(2.65)=3, reconstructs as 0.60.60.6, and has error +0.07+0.07+0.07. If one value is 8.48.48.4 and forces the same scale, then s=1.2s = 1.2s=1.2; 0.530.530.53 rounds to zero. The exceptional value has consumed the grid's useful resolution.

Clipping the range below the largest observed magnitude can reduce rounding error for common values but makes the tail saturate. The best threshold minimizes an objective measured on representative data; it is rarely guaranteed by the tensor's maximum alone. For a linear layer, a more relevant objective than raw weight mean-square error is the output error ∥XW−XW^∥2\|XW-X\hat W\|^2∥XW−XW^∥2. [2] [9]

Derivation: rounding noise, clipping error, and why range has an optimum

For a uniform nearest-rounding quantizer with step Δ and no clipping, write x̂=x+ε. Every value lies within half a step of a grid point, so |ε|≤Δ/2. If the input density is approximately constant inside many bins, the position within a bin is approximately uniform. Under this high-resolution approximation:

E[ε]≈1Δ∫−Δ/2Δ/2ε dε=0,E[ε2]≈1Δ∫−Δ/2Δ/2ε2 dε=Δ212.\begin{aligned}\mathbb E[\varepsilon]&\approx\frac1\Delta\int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2}\varepsilon\,d\varepsilon=0,\\\mathbb E[\varepsilon^2]&\approx\frac1\Delta\int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2}\varepsilon^2\,d\varepsilon=\frac{\Delta^2}{12}.\end{aligned}E[ε]E[ε2]​≈Δ1​∫−Δ/2Δ/2​εdε=0,≈Δ1​∫−Δ/2Δ/2​ε2dε=12Δ2​.​

The bound is deterministic; the zero-mean and variance statements are distributional approximations. Few levels, strong spikes at particular values, shared scales, and clipping can invalidate the uniform-noise model. Quantization errors are deterministic functions of the tensor unless explicit random rounding is introduced.

For a symmetric input density f and clipping interval [−a,a], let M=2ᵇ reconstruction levels include the endpoints and Δ=2a/(M−1). A useful approximate distortion splits ordinary rounding from overload:

D(a)≈Δ(a)212Pr⁡(∣X∣≤a)+2∫a∞(x−a)2f(x) dx.D(a)\approx\frac{\Delta(a)^2}{12}\Pr(|X|\le a)+2\int_a^\infty(x-a)^2f(x)\,dx.D(a)≈12Δ(a)2​Pr(∣X∣≤a)+2∫a∞​(x−a)2f(x)dx.

Increasing a makes the step wider and raises rounding error on ordinary values, but reduces the tail error. The second term's derivative is −4∫ₐ∞(x−a)f(x)dx because the integrand is zero at the moving lower endpoint. The first term has both a step-size derivative and a changing probability mass. Equating their sum to zero gives an interior optimum when one exists; setting a to the largest observed sample is not generally optimal.

This analysis explains the purpose of clipping calibration without proving that MSE-optimal clipping is task-optimal. A rare outlier aligned with an important activation direction can have a small frequency but a large layer-output cost. Replace the scalar distortion with the appropriate output/sensitivity objective when those directions matter.

Exercise — A deterministic bound is not a noise model

For step Δ=0.2, compute the maximum absolute error and the high-resolution MSE estimate. If every input already lies on the quantization grid, what is the actual MSE?

Show worked solution

The maximum absolute error is 0.1. The uniform-bin estimate is 0.2²/12=1/300≈0.003333. If all inputs lie exactly on grid points and none clips, actual MSE is zero. The deterministic bound remains true, while the uniform-within-bin assumption does not describe this input distribution.

1.2 Granularity buys accuracy with metadata

A scale group is the set of values sharing a scale. Per-tensor quantization shares one over a whole tensor. Per-channel uses a different scale for each row or column, depending on layout. Per-group or per-block schemes split a dimension into fixed-size groups. Smaller groups localize outliers, but every group needs scale metadata and can make kernels more complicated.

Bideal=Nb8  bytes,beffective≈b+Bscale,bitsG+Bzero,bitsG+other metadata bits per weight.\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{ideal}}&=\frac{Nb}{8}\;\mathrm{bytes},\\b_{\mathrm{effective}}&\approx b+\frac{B_{\mathrm{scale,bits}}}{G}+\frac{B_{\mathrm{zero,bits}}}{G}\\&\quad+\text{other metadata bits per weight}.\end{aligned}Bideal​beffective​​=8Nb​bytes,≈b+GBscale,bits​​+GBzero,bits​​+other metadata bits per weight.​

Example: four-bit weights, groups of 128, and one 16-bit scale per group need 4+16/128=4.1254 + 16/128 = 4.1254+16/128=4.125 bits per weight before alignment, optional zero points, and high-precision exceptions. A nominal 7-billion-parameter model would have 3.5 GB3.5\,\mathrm{GB}3.5GB of pure 4-bit payload or about 3.61 GB3.61\,\mathrm{GB}3.61GB with those scales, using decimal GB. Neither is a complete GPU memory estimate: embeddings, norms, padding, runtime buffers, and KV cache also occupy memory.

Practical caution: “per-channel” names an axis, not a quality guarantee. For Y=XWY=XWY=XW, scaling input feature jjj affects row jjj of WWW; scaling output channels affects columns. In the transposed convention V=W⊤V=W^\top V=W⊤, these axis names reverse. Confusing axes can make an apparently reasonable quantizer wrong for the matrix layout.
