What the lab cannot tell you

It visualizes scalar reconstruction error. Real inference quality depends on which values connect to important activation channels, the correlations among columns, the next layer, and task behavior. A lower scalar MSE is useful evidence, but it is not a guarantee of lower perplexity or better answers.

2Why LLMs resist naive quantization

The problem is distribution shape, not simply model size.

Activation outliers. A few feature dimensions can be much larger than their neighbors and recur across tokens. One shared activation scale gives those features range while pushing ordinary values toward zero. LLM.int8() isolates outlier dimensions for a higher-precision path; SmoothQuant transforms the layer so the activation range becomes easier to quantize. These are different remedies for the same failure mode. [1] [4]

Unequal importance. A small weight's rounding error can be important if the corresponding input feature is often large. For Y=XWY=XWY=XW, a perturbation ΔW\Delta WΔW creates ΔY=XΔW\Delta Y=X\Delta WΔY=XΔW. Across calibration samples, the error objective is ∥XΔW∥2\|X\Delta W\|^2∥XΔW∥2; the matrix X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X tells us how strongly input dimensions affect output error. This motivates GPTQ's approximate second-order correction and AWQ's activation-aware channel protection. [2] [3]

Accumulation and feedback. Quantized projection errors flow through attention, residual paths, nonlinearities, and many layers. During generation, a changed token can also change every subsequent input. A quantizer that looks acceptable on one layer or one short prompt may fail on long-context retrieval, code, arithmetic, or a rare output format. An empirical evaluation across tasks found that memory savings can coincide with slower inference and that perplexity is an incomplete proxy for some downstream behavior. [14]

3The method families

“PTQ” means post-training quantization. It can use calibration examples and optimize scales or reconstruction without retraining the whole original model.

3.1 Weight-only PTQ: round, protect, compensate

MethodCore ideaWhat it needsWhat to remember
RTNChoose scales, then round to nearest.Weights; perhaps calibration for clipping.Necessary baseline; often strong at 8 bits, weaker at very low bits.
GPTQ [2]Quantize columns sequentially and compensate rounding error in remaining columns using an approximate inverse Hessian from calibration activations.Representative layer inputs and an offline quantization pass.Targets layer output reconstruction; packing/kernel is a separate choice.
AWQ [3]Use activation statistics to identify salient weight channels; scale them before quantization and apply the inverse transformation elsewhere.Representative activations; no gradient descent in the paper's method.Salience comes from the input, not simply largest weights.
SpQR [10]Keep exceptional weights in a sparse higher-precision side structure.Outlier selection and a runtime able to consume the representation.Exceptions improve fidelity but add indices and irregular work.

GPTQ, AWQ, and RTN may all produce “4-bit weights,” yet their serialized layouts and output quality can differ. Also, AWQ is an algorithm, while a label such as W4A16 states operand precision. Neither names the exact hardware kernel. The AWQ paper reports speedups with its TinyChat implementation; those numbers are specific to its models, devices, and comparison point. [3]

3.2 Weight and activation quantization

LLM.int8() quantizes the bulk of matrix multiplication to INT8 and routes a very small number of outlier feature dimensions through 16-bit arithmetic. That preserves important features, with the cost of a second path and mixed-precision bookkeeping. [1]

SmoothQuant uses an exact diagonal reparameterization before rounding. For positive channel scales sjs_jsj​, divide activation channel jjj by sjs_jsj​ and multiply the matching weight row by sjs_jsj​. The original floating-point layer is unchanged, but activation peaks are smaller and weight ranges larger. Its paper studies W8A8 INT8 inference; the transformed model still needs calibration and a suitable kernel to deliver speed. [4]

Y=XW=(XD−1)(DW),D=diag⁡(s1,…,sd),sj>0.Quantize XD−1 and DW separately after transformation.\begin{aligned}Y&=XW=(XD^{-1})(DW),\\D&=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_d),\qquad s_j>0.\\&\text{Quantize $XD^{-1}$ and $DW$ separately after transformation.}\end{aligned}YD​=XW=(XD−1)(DW),=diag(s1​,…,sd​),sj​>0.Quantize XD−1 and DW separately after transformation.​

FP8 is another W8A8 route, but “FP8” alone does not specify scaling granularity or whether activation scales are static or calculated at runtime. Hardware-accelerated implementations support several choices. Compare the exact checkpoint recipe and kernel, not the format name. [17] [19]

3.3 Rotation, codebooks, and training-aware routes

Rotations aim to spread concentrated magnitude over dimensions while preserving the unquantized function. QuaRot uses orthogonal transformations to make weights, activations, and KV cache amenable to four-bit inference; SpinQuant learns rotations for better quantized accuracy. A rotation may be folded into adjacent linear layers, while some placements require runtime work. [7] [8]

Nonuniform and vector codebooks replace a uniform scalar grid with learned representatives or multi-value codes. QuIP# uses incoherence processing plus lattice codebooks; AQLM combines multiple codebooks for very low-bit weight compression. They extend the accuracy frontier in the papers' settings, but lookup/decode cost and available kernels still determine serving value. [11] [12]

Quantization-aware training (QAT) exposes the training process to fake rounding or low-precision effects, allowing parameter updates to adapt. LLM-QAT demonstrates this for weights, activations, and KV cache. It needs more training effort than typical PTQ. BitNet b1.58 trains ternary weights as a native architecture; it is not a recipe for converting an arbitrary pretrained BF16 transformer to a high-quality 1.58-bit model. [13] [20]

QLoRA solves a different practical problem: fine-tuning a frozen base model stored in four-bit NF4 while training low-rank adapters, using compute at higher precision. Its NF4 codebook, double quantization of constants, and paged optimizers save training memory. It does not imply INT4 tensor-core inference or that the resulting base plus adapter is automatically the best serving format. [5]

Research development: the bottleneck changes, so the winning method changes

The chronology below follows first public reports; a later conference year or revised PDF does not move the original contribution forward in time. This is a map of the main mechanisms, not a claim that one family supersedes every other. Weight-only compression, integer GEMM, fine-tuning memory, and low-precision pretraining solve different optimization problems.

StageLandmark contributions and variantsQuestion that defines the stageWhat the next stage adds
2022: make eight bits reliableZeroQuant; LLM.int8(); FP8 formats; SmoothQuantWhich activation axes and outliers break ordinary quantization, and can a practical GEMM consume the result?Four-bit weights need a better error objective than magnitude alone.
Late 2022–2023: exploit calibration geometryGPTQ from OBQ; AWQ; SpQR; OmniQuant; SignRound; HQQWhich rounding errors matter, and should we compensate, rescale, isolate, or optimize them?At two bits, independent scalar grids waste representational capacity.
2023–2024: extreme weight compressionQuIP → QuIP#; AQLM; residual/additive vector codesCan we reshape the weight/error geometry and encode correlated vectors together?Weight-only success leaves the activation and KV bottlenecks.
2024–2025: transform the complete inference graphQuaRot; SpinQuant; DuQuant; FlatQuantWhere can an exact transform remove outliers, and where does it require online work?Hardware microscaling makes the scale-group boundary part of the algorithm.
Parallel training branch, 2023–2026QLoRA; LLM-QAT; BitNet b1.58; NVFP4 pretraining; SignRoundV2; DuQuant++Which parameters, gradients, or rounding rules must adapt, and to which executable format?Evaluate long training horizons, real kernels, and task-sensitive mixed precision.

The recurring progression is identify a failure mode → choose the right geometry → constrain the representation → implement the execution path. A lower nominal bit width alone does not establish progress. For example, a two-bit vector code can have excellent quality per checkpoint byte but require custom decompression; a four-bit floating operand can execute directly on newer matrix units but requires a different calibration rule and scale layout.

3.4 2022: from range selection to outlier-aware GEMM

Problems and objectives. The immediate obstacle is that a few large activation channels consume the range of a shared low-bit quantizer, making naive integer GEMM inaccurate. This stage explores better scale granularity, explicit high-precision outlier paths, and equivalent rescaling that moves range from activations into weights.

ZeroQuant: granularity must agree with the kernel

Core idea. Match group-wise weight and fine-grained activation quantization to efficient low-precision kernels, with layer-wise distillation used where needed to recover quality. The recipe treats executable granularity and reconstruction accuracy as connected choices.

ZeroQuant begins with two observations: token activation ranges vary, and different output neurons have different weight ranges. Sharing one scale over either entire tensor discards useful levels. It therefore combines dynamic per-token activation quantization with grouped weight quantization chosen to suit GPU matrix tiles. This is more than a statistical choice: a scale configuration that is cheap to describe can be expensive to apply if it changes within a hardware dot product. [28]

For a row-input linear layer, write X∈RT×dX\in\mathbb R^{T\times d}X∈RT×d, W∈Rd×oW\in\mathbb R^{d\times o}W∈Rd×o, and Y=XWY=XWY=XW. If activation scale ata_tat​ depends only on token and weight scale bkb_kbk​ only on output channel, an integer accumulator can be rescaled once at the end: Y^t,k=atbk∑j(qX)t,j(qW)j,k\hat Y_{t,k}=a_tb_k\sum_j(q_X)_{t,j}(q_W)_{j,k}Y^t,k​=at​bk​∑j​(qX​)t,j​(qW​)j,k​. If the product of scales varies with reduction index jjj, one final multiplier is insufficient. The kernel must form separately scaled partial sums, transform the operands first, or use hardware with native block scaling. This algebra explains why “per-channel activation quantization works” is not yet an efficient W8A8 implementation.

Read the figure. The left chain writes outputs between normalization/GeLU, quantization, GEMM, and dequantization. The right chain fuses quantization into the producer and dequantization into the GEMM epilogue. It removes intermediate memory traffic and launches while retaining the necessary scale arithmetic. The INT8 multiply accumulates into INT32 before reconstruction to a higher-precision output. This distinction between operand precision, accumulator precision, and output storage recurs in FP8/FP4 hardware.

ZeroQuant also introduces layer-by-layer knowledge distillation for harder precision settings. A full-precision block is the temporary teacher for its quantized counterpart; matching block outputs avoids simultaneously training a complete separate teacher and student. The optimization cost and data requirement are different from ordinary range-only PTQ. Its original smaller-model and mixed W4/W8 experiments should not be extrapolated into a universal four-bit solution for current models. The lasting contribution is the coupled design of quantization granularity, local recovery, and fused kernels. [28]

LLM.int8(): preserve a small subspace explicitly

Core idea. Separate large outlier feature dimensions into a higher-precision computation and run the remaining matrix product in INT8. Add the two contributions so a small difficult subspace does not set the numeric range for the whole operation.

The LLM.int8() paper identifies recurring high-magnitude feature dimensions whose contribution cannot simply be clipped away. For the outlier set OOO, decompose the multiplication exactly before rounding:

XW=X:,OWO,:+X:,O‾WO‾,:,Y^=MatMul⁡FP16(X:,O,WO,:)+Dequant⁡ ⁣(MatMul⁡INT8(X:,O‾,WO‾,:)).\begin{aligned}XW&=X_{:,\mathcal O}W_{\mathcal O,:}+X_{:,\overline{\mathcal O}}W_{\overline{\mathcal O},:},\\\widehat Y&=\operatorname{MatMul}_{\mathrm{FP16}}(X_{:,\mathcal O},W_{\mathcal O,:})\\&\quad+\operatorname{Dequant}\!\left(\operatorname{MatMul}_{\mathrm{INT8}}(X_{:,\overline{\mathcal O}},W_{\overline{\mathcal O},:})\right).\end{aligned}XWY​=X:,O​WO,:​+X:,O​WO,:​,=MatMulFP16​(X:,O​,WO,:​)+Dequant(MatMulINT8​(X:,O​,WO,:​)).​

Read the figure. Yellow columns of the input correspond to yellow rows of the weight matrix. They leave the main INT8 route together; retaining only large activation values without the matching weights would not compute the right contribution. The upper route uses vector-wise scaling and an INT32 accumulation, and the lower route produces the protected FP16 contribution. The final addition joins two output matrices of identical shape. [1]

The criterion concerns feature magnitude, not the magnitude of individual weights or a generic sparse mask. The paper finds that a tiny set of dimensions accounts for a disproportionate part of the failure at larger model sizes. Its observation that more than 99.9% of values can remain in the INT8 path belongs to those evaluated architectures and thresholds. Models with different training distributions can have different outlier structure. Two paths also mean gathering, extra launches, and a second matmul; an accuracy-preserving representation can still lose latency at small shapes.

SmoothQuant: pay for the activation range with weight range

Core idea. Rescale activation channels downward and the corresponding weight channels upward with an algebraically equivalent diagonal transformation. This transfers quantization difficulty toward the easier-to-quantize weights so both operands can use INT8.

SmoothQuant replaces the split path with an exact diagonal reparameterization. Choose positive sjs_jsj​, define D=diag⁡(s)D=\operatorname{diag}(s)D=diag(s), and use XW=(XD−1)(DW)XW=(XD^{-1})(DW)XW=(XD−1)(DW). In this guide's row-input notation, DDD scales rows of W, each corresponding to one input feature. The paper's column-input convention transposes these axes. A common scale rule is:

aj=max⁡t ∈ calibration tokens∣Xt,j∣,wj=max⁡k ∈ output channels∣Wj,k∣,sj=ajαwj1−α,0≤α≤1.\begin{aligned}a_j&=\max_{t\,\in\,\text{calibration tokens}}|X_{t,j}|,\\w_j&=\max_{k\,\in\,\text{output channels}}|W_{j,k}|,\\s_j&=\frac{a_j^\alpha}{w_j^{1-\alpha}},\qquad 0\le\alpha\le1.\end{aligned}aj​wj​sj​​=t∈calibration tokensmax​∣Xt,j​∣,=k∈output channelsmax​∣Wj,k​∣,=wj1−α​ajα​​,0≤α≤1.​

Read the figure. The left pair plots activation magnitudes over tokens and channels. The high ridges shrink after smoothing. The right pair plots weights, whose initially easy range expands. The vertical scales differ between panels, so equal apparent height is not equal numerical magnitude. SmoothQuant deliberately transfers quantization difficulty between operands; it does not reduce every range simultaneously. The transformation is exact in real arithmetic, while the two rounding operations introduce the actual approximation. [4]

Large α\alpha α aggressively smooths activations but can make weights hard to quantize. Small α\alpha α protects weights while retaining activation outliers. This explains both the search for a balance and the failure of treating α=0.5\alpha =0.5α=0.5 as universal. Folding the inverse scale into a preceding normalization or linear layer avoids an extra runtime operation when graph structure permits it. With multiple consumers, all paths using the transformed activation must remain consistent.

The paper distinguishes O1 dynamic per-token activation scales, O2 dynamic per-tensor scales, and O3 static per-tensor scales. O3 reduces runtime scale estimation but relies more strongly on calibration. Its W8A8 label primarily concerns expensive linear/BMM operations; norms, softmax, and other sensitive operations need not become INT8. FP8 then provides a parallel hardware route with a nonuniform floating grid, but does not eliminate the need to decide scale granularity and calibration policy. The datatype atlas explains why E4M3 and E5M2 make different range/precision trades. [4] [25]

3.5 Late 2022–2023: choose which weight errors to tolerate

Problems and objectives. At three or four weight bits, equal numeric errors have unequal effects on layer outputs. This stage asks how calibration activations and sensitivity estimates should guide rounding, channel protection, sparse exceptions, or learned reconstruction parameters while keeping the pretrained model largely fixed.

GPTQ: the input covariance defines the cost of rounding

Core idea. Round weights sequentially under a calibration-based layer reconstruction metric and compensate each rounding error by adjusting remaining weights. Approximate second-order information determines which compensating changes best preserve the layer’s output.

Raw weight MSE assumes every input direction matters equally. Instead, consider an output column www and calibration matrix XXX. Its reconstruction loss is L=(w−q)⊤X⊤X(w−q)\mathcal L=(w-q)^\top X^\top X(w-q)L=(w−q)⊤X⊤X(w−q). If two input channels are strongly correlated, a positive error in one may be canceled by a negative error in the other. GPTQ uses this structure to round weights sequentially and update those that remain free. Its curvature proxy is H=2X⊤X+λIH=2X^\top X+\lambda IH=2X⊤X+λI; damping stabilizes ill-conditioned calibration statistics. [2]

To follow the original algorithm without mixing axes, define V=W⊤V=W^\top V=W⊤: V rows are outputs and V columns are inputs. GPTQ quantizes V:,jV_{:,j}V:,j​ together across output rows. If one remaining scalar vjv_jvj​ must become qjq_jqj​, the constrained quadratic minimizer is:

min⁡δ12δTHδsubject to δj=qj−vj,δ=(qj−vj)(H−1):,j(H−1)j,j,ΔLmin⁡=(qj−vj)22(H−1)j,j.\begin{aligned}\min_\delta\quad&\frac12\delta^{\mathsf T}H\delta\quad\text{subject to }\delta_j=q_j-v_j,\\\delta&=\frac{(q_j-v_j)(H^{-1})_{:,j}}{(H^{-1})_{j,j}},\\\Delta L_{\min}&=\frac{(q_j-v_j)^2}{2(H^{-1})_{j,j}}.\end{aligned}δmin​δΔLmin​​21​δTHδsubject to δj​=qj​−vj​,=(H−1)j,j​(qj​−vj​)(H−1):,j​​,=2(H−1)j,j​(qj​−vj​)2​.​

The off-diagonal inverse-curvature entries tell the algorithm where compensation is available. A small scalar rounding error is not automatically cheap: if (H−1)j,j(H^{-1})_{j,j}(H−1)j,j​ is small, changing that coordinate is expensive under the observed inputs. Once a coordinate is fixed, it must be removed from the free subproblem. Reusing the original full inverse after every step would be incorrect.

Read the figure. Orange weight columns are already committed, purple columns remain adjustable, and the bold block is processed together. The triangular structure on the left is a Cholesky representation of inverse-curvature information. GPTQ shares a column order across all output rows, performs sequential corrections inside a block, and postpones the large update to later columns until the block finishes. That final operation is a matrix multiplication, making much better use of a GPU than many tiny rank-one operations. [2]

The predecessor OBQ chose a greedy order separately for each output row. That is attractive mathematically but makes every row carry a different evolving inverse problem. GPTQ's common order, lazy block updates, and stable Cholesky formulation make the reconstruction procedure tractable at LLM scale. In Cholesky form, the algorithm divides the current error by a diagonal factor and uses the corresponding factor row for corrections; these values should not be confused with raw H−1H^{-1}H−1 entries in the constrained derivation.

Variants change ordering and grouping. Activation-order heuristics visit high-importance input directions first, often using the Gram diagonal. Group size controls scale reuse; smaller groups spend additional metadata for local resolution. Static group layouts preserve contiguous packing, while regrouping after a permutation can complicate the kernel. Thus “GPTQ, 4 bit, group 128” still leaves meaningful choices unresolved. Its original work compresses weights; a speedup comes from reducing weight traffic and a suitable fused kernel, not from automatically turning a W4A16 operation into native INT4 arithmetic. Calibration drift and accumulation across layers remain limitations.

AWQ: protect salient channels without an FP16 exception path

Core idea. Identify activation-salient channels and search equivalent per-channel scales that reduce their quantization error. The final representation remains uniformly low-bit rather than requiring a separate high-precision path for those channels.

AWQ first tests which small subset of channels should be preserved accurately. Selection from activation magnitude helps much more than selection from large weights alone: a modest weight on a frequently large feature can matter more than a large weight on an inactive feature. Keeping those channels in FP16 demonstrates salience but would introduce a mixed-precision execution path. AWQ's deployable solution scales the salient channels before ordinary grouped weight quantization. [3]

Read the figure. The left panel applies direct three-bit rounding. The middle panel retains activation-selected channels in FP16, exposing their importance but creating irregular execution. The right panel expands those same channels before rounding into a regular integer tensor. Its reported perplexities are one OPT-6.7B INT3 group-128 example, not universal performance values. The central experimental result is that the selection criterion matters.

Using aj=mean⁡t∣Xt,j∣a_j=\operatorname{mean}_t|X_{t,j}|aj​=meant​∣Xt,j​∣, AWQ searches sj=ajαs_j=a_j^\alphasj​=ajα​ and minimizes the layer reconstruction error of (XD−1)Q(DW)(XD^{-1})Q(DW)(XD−1)Q(DW). A salient weight's rounding error in the transformed coordinates is divided by sjs_jsj​ on returning to the original function. But scaling a maximum can enlarge a shared group's step and worsen other channels. The paper's separate OPT-6.7B scaling example improves WikiText-2 perplexity from 23.54 to 11.92 at scale 2, then worsens to 12.36 at scale 4. More protection is not monotonically better. Range clipping is another calibrated decision.

GPTQ and AWQ operate on different freedoms: GPTQ adjusts unrounded weights to cancel committed errors; AWQ changes coordinates and scales before rounding. AWQ+GPTQ therefore makes conceptual sense and is evaluated in the paper. Neither method names a storage container. TinyChat's reported acceleration also includes fused operations and device-specific packing; the same quantized values in an unfused implementation can be slower. AWQ's ARM NEON packing is a useful reminder that an encoding friendly to one vector instruction may need repacking on another device.

SpQR: protect sensitivity, then pay for the indices

Core idea. Quantize the bulk of weights while retaining especially sensitive outliers in a sparse higher-precision representation. Quantizing the quantization metadata further lowers size, but exception values and indices remain part of the effective bit budget.

SpQR combines grouped low-bit dense weights, second-order sensitivity analysis, sparse high-precision exceptions, and another level of quantization for the scales/zero points. The sparse component is selected because some weights are costly to quantize under the output reconstruction objective, not merely because they are numerically large. Small groups improve accuracy but can make ordinary metadata dominate; quantizing that metadata helps fund the exception structure. [10]

Read the figure. This is a log-sensitivity map from LLaMA-65B's last attention layer, with output dimensions on rows and input dimensions on columns. Dark regions are more sensitive. Zooms show head-related structure, rotary-related patterns, row/column patterns, and isolated elements. A single rule such as “protect the largest 1% of weights” cannot describe all of them. The map explains why sensitivity-aware exceptions can help even after channel scaling.

A generic additive exception encoding has bNbNbN dense bits plus r(bhi+bidx)r(b_{\mathrm{hi}}+b_{\mathrm{idx}})r(bhi​+bidx​) exception bits, group statistics, and row-pointer overhead. If dense placeholders are omitted, the dense term instead covers N−rN-rN−r; implementations differ. A quoted three-bit dense component can therefore produce substantially more than three effective bits per weight. The runtime also has to combine a dense low-bit result with sparse corrections. SpQR is attractive when accuracy gained per exception pays for irregular accesses; the breakpoint depends on exception density, matrix shape, and sparse-kernel efficiency.

SqueezeLLM: sensitivity-weighted nonuniform scalar levels

Core idea. Choose nonuniform scalar code levels using sensitivity-weighted clustering rather than equal numeric spacing. Isolate sparse difficult values so the dense codebook can represent the remaining weights more accurately.

SqueezeLLM combines a nonuniform scalar codebook with a sparse side structure. It approximates weight sensitivity using diagonal Fisher information and solves a weighted clustering problem: choose representatives to minimize ∑ihi(wi−cindexi)2\sum_i h_i(w_i-c_{\mathrm{index}_i})^2∑i​hi​(wi​−cindexi​​)2. The large hih_ihi​ values make errors expensive even if the corresponding weights are not extreme. This differs from GPTQ's full input-covariance compensation and from AQLM's multi-value additive codebooks. Separating sensitive or large outliers lets the dense codebook spend more representatives on the bulk distribution. [40]

Its dense part therefore stores short lookup indices, not conventional uniformly spaced INT3 values. The kernel must reconstruct a lookup value and combine sparse corrections. Its reported A6000 gains target bandwidth-dominated generation; they should not be generalized to large prefill GEMMs without measuring the lookup implementation. The connection to KVQuant is methodological: both use sensitivity-weighted nonuniform levels and outlier isolation, applied to tensors with different lifetimes and scale axes.

OmniQuant and SignRound: optimize a compact calibration problem

Core idea. OmniQuant learns clipping and equivalent transformation parameters through block reconstruction; SignRound optimizes rounding decisions with sign-based updates on a calibration objective. Both turn selected quantization choices into a small optimization problem instead of accepting nearest rounding unchanged.

OmniQuant freezes the pretrained weights and learns clipping strengths plus equivalent scale/shift transformations against a transformer-block reconstruction objective. It learns upper/lower clipping factors γ,β∈[0,1]\gamma,\beta\in[0,1]γ,β∈[0,1], giving a step proportional to γmax⁡W−βmin⁡W2b−1\frac{\gamma\max W-\beta\min W}{2^b-1}2b−1γmaxW−βminW​. Separate factors allow an asymmetric range. The shift extension is also exact before rounding: (X−c)D−1(DW)+(bias+cW)=XW+bias(X-c)D^{-1}(DW)+(\mathrm{bias}+cW)=XW+\mathrm{bias}(X−c)D−1(DW)+(bias+cW)=XW+bias. Matching a whole block can capture interactions that independent matrix reconstruction misses. [9]

Read the figure. Snowflakes mark frozen weights and flames identify calibration parameters. Pink transform/clipping boxes are optimized, while green quantization boxes simulate their consequence. Transformations surround both projection layers and attention operands. The deployed graph can absorb the learned equivalent parameters into weights/biases or quantizer parameters; the calibration diagram is not a list of extra inference modules. That folding is the reason this remains practical PTQ despite using gradients.

The core objective is min⁡θ∥F(W,X)−Fquant(W,X;θ)∥2\min_\theta\|F(W,X)-F_{\mathrm{quant}}(W,X;\theta)\|^2minθ​∥F(W,X)−Fquant​(W,X;θ)∥2, with θ\theta θ much smaller than the original weight set. It requires an offline optimization budget and representative data. It is not guaranteed to optimize downstream task loss, and very low-bit joint activation/weight settings can still be difficult. A method using gradients during calibration should not be classified as full model retraining solely because autograd appears in its implementation.

SignRound, implemented in the AutoRound toolkit, introduces trainable offsets before rounding as well as clipping parameters. An offset needs to cross a decision boundary, not converge to a uniquely meaningful real number. Signed-gradient updates exploit that structure: v←v−ηsign⁡ ⁣(∂L∂v)v\leftarrow v-\eta\operatorname{sign}\!\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial v}\right)v←v−ηsign(∂v∂L​), with clipping to the allowed offset interval. The resulting checkpoint contains the selected integer codes, not the learned offset tensor. It is a different optimization route from GPTQ's sequential curvature compensation. The 2025 SignRoundV2 work adds scale pre-search, stabilization and sensitivity-guided mixed precision; comparisons must state whether the bit allocation is uniform or adaptive. [29] [30]

HQQ is a useful calibration-free counterpoint. It fits quantizer parameters directly to weights with a robust p<1p<1p<1 error penalty. Half-quadratic splitting introduces an auxiliary error, alternates a shrinkage update with a zero-point update, and keeps the scale fixed in the described solver. It uses no activation covariance, avoiding calibration dependence and reducing conversion cost. That also means it cannot directly distinguish directions important to the actual input distribution. Its regular dequantization form can use suitable conventional kernels. Treat the choice as a trade between conversion cost, data access and accuracy rather than assuming calibration is always available. [31]

Derivation: layer reconstruction and GPTQ compensation from one constraint

Fix a column-vector convention: y=Wx, W∈ℝ^(m×d), and calibration samples form X∈ℝ^(d×n). Consider one output row w∈ℝ^d written as a column for the optimization. A weight perturbation δ changes that output across samples by Xᵀδ. Thus:

L(δ)=1n∥XTδ∥22=δT ⁣(XXTn)δ=12δTHδ,H=2XXTn.\begin{aligned}L(\delta)&=\frac1n\lVert X^{\mathsf T}\delta\rVert_2^2=\delta^{\mathsf T}\!\left(\frac{XX^{\mathsf T}}n\right)\delta=\frac12\delta^{\mathsf T}H\delta,\\H&=\frac{2XX^{\mathsf T}}n.\end{aligned}L(δ)H​=n1​∥XTδ∥22​=δT(nXXT​)δ=21​δTHδ,=n2XXT​.​

This is an exact quadratic for a frozen linear layer and fixed inputs, not a second-order approximation to the entire network's task loss. It shows which perturbation directions the calibration data expose. If n<d or some input directions never occur, H can be singular; adding λI stabilizes inversion but changes the objective by an L2 penalty on δ.

Suppose weight coordinate j is forced to its quantized value qj, so δj=qj−wj=e. Allow all other still-unfixed coordinates to compensate, and assume their restricted H is positive definite. Introduce multiplier ν:

min⁡δ12δTHδsubject to ejTδ=e,∇δ ⁣[12δTHδ+ν(ejTδ−e)]=Hδ+νej=0,δ=−νH−1ej,e=−ν(H−1)jj⟹ν=−e(H−1)jj,δ∗=eH−1ej(H−1)jj,Lmin⁡=e22(H−1)jj.\begin{aligned}\min_\delta\quad&\frac12\delta^{\mathsf T}H\delta\quad\text{subject to }e_j^{\mathsf T}\delta=e,\\\nabla_\delta\!\left[\frac12\delta^{\mathsf T}H\delta+\nu(e_j^{\mathsf T}\delta-e)\right]&=H\delta+\nu e_j=0,\\\delta&=-\nu H^{-1}e_j,\\e&=-\nu(H^{-1})_{jj}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\nu=-\frac e{(H^{-1})_{jj}},\\\delta^*&=\frac{eH^{-1}e_j}{(H^{-1})_{jj}},\\L_{\min}&=\frac{e^2}{2(H^{-1})_{jj}}.\end{aligned}δmin​∇δ​[21​δTHδ+ν(ejT​δ−e)]δeδ∗Lmin​​21​δTHδsubject to ejT​δ=e,=Hδ+νej​=0,=−νH−1ej​,=−ν(H−1)jj​⟹ν=−(H−1)jj​e​,=(H−1)jj​eH−1ej​​,=2(H−1)jj​e2​.​

Here eⱼ denotes a basis vector, distinct from scalar e. The j-th component equals the forced change; other components shift according to input correlations. If an implementation defines error as wj−qj, the same update appears with a minus sign. Apparent sign disagreements often come from this convention.

After fixing j, future steps optimize in the remaining coordinate space. Block processing, inverse-factor updates and damping make this practical, but do not remove the dependence on calibration inputs. A low reconstruction loss on X gives no guarantee in directions absent from X. This is also why equal scalar weight MSE can produce unequal layer error.

Exercise — Solve a two-weight rounding step

Let H=[[2,1],[1,2]] and force δ₁=1. Find the optimal δ₂ and compare the loss with leaving δ₂=0.

Show worked solution

H⁻¹=(1/3)[[2,−1],[−1,2]]. Therefore δ*=(1,−1/2). Direct substitution gives L=½[2·1²+2·1·(−1/2)+2·(1/4)]=3/4. With δ₂=0, L=1. Correlated inputs permit another weight to absorb part of the error. The remaining loss is nonzero because the constraint cannot be undone completely under positive-definite H.

3.6 2023–2024: incoherence and vector codes below four bits

Problems and objectives. Below four bits, independently rounding weights can leave too little representational freedom even with good scales. This branch changes the coordinate system or shares codewords across weight groups, spending transformation and dictionary complexity to reduce error under the layer’s input-dependent metric.

QuIP → QuIP#: quantize the error geometry in a better basis

Core idea. Transform weights and their error metric into a more incoherent basis so difficult directions are less concentrated. QuIP# combines structured randomized transforms with a lattice-based codebook to make very low-bit reconstruction more effective.

At two bits a scalar has only four codes. Small clipping refinements cannot recover the representational capacity that is absent. QuIP argues that coordinate coherence matters: large entries in weights or concentrated eigenvectors of the input covariance make a scalar grid fragile. Orthogonal preprocessing spreads this concentration, while LDL-based adaptive rounding accounts for input correlations. QuIP# replaces expensive structured random transforms with randomized Hadamard transforms and introduces an eight-dimensional lattice codebook. [11] [32]

In column-input notation y=Vxy=Vxy=Vx, let UUU and RRR be orthogonal transforms for output and input spaces. Set V~=UVR⊤\tilde V=UVR^\topV~=UVR⊤, H~=RHR⊤\tilde H=RHR^\topH~=RHR⊤, and x~=Rx\tilde x=Rxx~=Rx. Then y=U⊤V~x~y=U^\top\tilde V\tilde xy=U⊤V~x~ before rounding, and the calibration-weighted error is preserved by the coordinate change. The purpose is to change which discrete approximation is easy, not to improve the unquantized network. A matrix with well-spread entries can still have important correlated directions, so flattening weight magnitudes alone is insufficient.

A normalized Hadamard transform has entries ±1/d\pm1/\sqrt d±1/d​; a random sign diagonal avoids repeatedly aligning with a structured input. Fast transforms cost O(dlog⁡d)O(d\log d)O(dlogd) additions, far less than a dense O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2) rotation. They can nevertheless matter for small batches and require careful handling when dimensions are not powers of two. QuIP# combines this preprocessing with block LDL feedback, so its code vectors are chosen under a correlated reconstruction objective rather than by independent nearest scalar rounding.

Read the figure. The horizontal axis is bits per scalar and the logarithmic vertical axis is elementwise MSE for a multivariate Gaussian. The E8-based curves improve distortion relative to scalar/half-integer alternatives at a comparable rate. This is a codebook geometry experiment, not a plot of LLM perplexity or end-to-end latency. It supports using a vector code after transforms make the distribution more suitable; it does not prove that every model becomes Gaussian.

The E8P construction encodes an eight-value vector with a 16-bit index: two payload bits per weight. Its structured symmetries permit a compact lookup representation, important because a naive table of all 2162^{16}216 vectors would consume much more fast memory. For three and four bits, QuIP# uses residual vector quantization: quantize once, encode the remaining error using another small codebook, and add the reconstructions. Scales, transform signs, padding and high-precision tensors still contribute to total storage. Block/end-to-end recovery options also change the result; compare an equally tuned version of each method. [11]

AQLM: learn sums of codewords under the input metric

Core idea. Represent each weight group as a sum of learned codewords selected from several codebooks. Optimize the representation against calibration-driven reconstruction error so multiple small indices can describe a richer vector than independent scalar rounding.

AQLM imports additive quantization from vector search and adapts it to layer output error. Split an output row into groups of ggg input weights. Each group is approximated by the sum of one vector from each of MMM codebooks, with 2B2^B2B entries per book. The index payload is MB/gMB/gMB/g bits per weight. Two 8-bit indices for a group of eight values give two payload bits per weight, while the learned codebooks and output scales cost additional memory. [12]

Read the figure. Blue blocks are stored indices, not low-bit floating values. Looking up the indices yields green vectors from several codebooks; those vectors are summed and then scaled per output row. The “weight matrix” at the far right is a conceptual reconstruction. A useful implementation decompresses into tiles or combines lookup with multiplication, avoiding persistent materialization of the full FP16 matrix.

AQLM initializes its codebooks with residual k-means. It then alternates three forms of recovery. First, discrete beam search changes indices while retaining several promising assignments. Second, gradient updates optimize the continuous codebooks and row scales with indices fixed. Third, block-level fine-tuning recovers interactions among separately compressed matrices. In all cases the input covariance matters: with ΔV=V−V^\Delta V=V-\hat VΔV=V−V^, the objective is tr⁡(ΔVHΔV⊤)\operatorname{tr}(\Delta V H\Delta V^\top)tr(ΔVHΔV⊤), where H=XX⊤H=XX^\top H=XX⊤ in the paper's column-input convention.

Expanding that quadratic explains why choosing the closest codeword by Euclidean distance is insufficient. The loss contains unary terms between original weights and codewords, plus pairwise terms between different selected codewords through HHH. A code that looks locally best can interact badly with the rest of the row. Beam search approximates this combinatorial problem; computing the input Gram matrix once lets it score updates without replaying all calibration tokens every time. Continuous codebook optimization is a coupled least-squares problem, implemented with iterative optimization in the paper.

QuIP# and AQLM therefore make different engineering bets. QuIP# uses a highly structured reusable lattice and fast transforms; AQLM learns additive codebooks tailored to a layer. Both add offline work and specialized decoding. More codebooks improve expressiveness but increase lookups, additions and metadata. At large GEMM batch sizes, dense tensor-core execution can dominate the economics; at batch-one decode, compact indices and fused decompression can be valuable. The same-model result comparison in §9.3 is the appropriate place to inspect their quality frontier.

3.7 2024–2026: transform the whole graph, then match the hardware group

Problems and objectives. Compressing isolated weights is insufficient when activations, attention state, and hardware scale groups remain difficult to quantize. The objective becomes an executable transformation of the computation graph: preserve full-precision algebra, improve local distributions, and match actual kernel group boundaries and operand formats.

QuaRot: computational invariance is a graph property

Core idea. Insert compatible orthogonal transformations through the network so outliers are spread across coordinates while the unquantized computation is preserved. Quantize the resulting weights, activations, and cache using the transformed graph and supported kernels.

QuaRot addresses weights, activations and KV together. An orthogonal transform can be absorbed into neighboring weights only when the intervening operations preserve the needed identity. RMS normalization without its learned diagonal scale satisfies RMSNorm⁡(xR)=RMSNorm⁡(x)R\operatorname{RMSNorm}(xR)=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(x)RRMSNorm(xR)=RMSNorm(x)R, because rotation preserves the vector norm. Absorbing the learned RMSNorm scale into following weights makes this identity usable across the residual stream. Arbitrary elementwise nonlinearities do not commute with a general rotation. [7]

Read the figure. The residual input and output are in the same rotated basis. The two incoming weight matrices undo that basis before the gate's nonlinearity; the down-projection restores the rotated residual basis. Crucially, an explicit online Hadamard appears after gating and before the down projection. It cannot simply be moved through the nonlinearity. Labels also distinguish INT4 operands from FP16 intermediate values; a W4A4KV4 model still contains operations and accumulations at higher precision.

QuaRot uses GPTQ on the transformed weights by default and dynamic rounding for activations. Its RTN ablation asks whether rotation alone is enough; the quality difference measures the remaining value of compensated rounding. Value vectors can be rotated per head while applying the inverse in the output projection, preserving the attention result. Queries and keys can receive the same orthogonal transform after RoPE, since (QR)(KR)⊤=QK⊤(QR)(KR)^\top =QK^\top (QR)(KR)⊤=QK⊤. Moving a generic rotation before RoPE is not equivalent because the matrices need not commute.

These placements define an execution contract: the newly generated key is transformed once and stored in that basis; later queries must use the compatible basis. Weight folding reduces online work, but the remaining Hadamard transforms, activation quantization and quantized attention kernels must be measured. The original paper's RTX 3090 speed/memory results include particular layer shapes, batch sizes and sequence lengths; they are not generic four-bit speed multipliers.

SpinQuant: the choice of orthogonal basis still matters

Core idea. Learn orthogonal rotations that improve the model’s behavior under quantization rather than accepting a fixed random basis. Apply weight quantization to the chosen rotated representation, preserving the distinction between exact basis changes and subsequent rounding error.

All orthogonal rotations preserve the floating-point network when correctly inserted, but they need not produce equally good quantized networks. SpinQuant explicitly measures that variation and learns two classes of foldable rotations: one for the residual stream and headwise value/output rotations. It leaves the expensive-to-fold online transforms as efficient Hadamards. The main experiments optimize rotations with activation quantization, then apply GPTQ to the rotated weights. This order is a substantive recipe detail. [8]

Read the figure. The violin width reflects variability over different random rotations, and the y-axis is average zero-shot commonsense reasoning accuracy for the paper's LLaMA-2-7B W4A4 setting. Hadamard initialization is substantially better than unrestricted random rotation in this experiment, but still varies. Cayley-optimized rotations cluster higher with less variation. A rotation that improves an outlier statistic does not uniquely determine downstream quality.

To remain orthogonal, optimization takes place on the orthogonal/Stiefel constraint set. For skew-symmetric AAA with A⊤=−AA^\top =-AA⊤=−A, a Cayley update Rnew=(I−ηA/2)−1(I+ηA/2)RR_{\mathrm{new}}=(I-\eta A/2)^{-1}(I+\eta A/2)RRnew​=(I−ηA/2)−1(I+ηA/2)R preserves orthogonality. Ordinary unconstrained gradient descent on RRR would lose the inverse-equals-transpose property and therefore invalidate exact folding. The paper uses an efficient iterative implementation of this update rather than requiring a generic dense inverse at every step. Calibration cost buys a better basis, while the runtime cost depends on which transforms can actually be merged.

DuQuant and FlatQuant: target the remaining shape of the distribution

Core idea. DuQuant uses outlier-guided block rotations and a balancing permutation to redistribute difficult magnitudes; FlatQuant learns more general invertible transforms under reconstruction objectives. Both improve the distribution seen by the quantizer, with different transform costs and constraints.

DuQuant distinguishes persistent channel outliers from rare, massive token-specific outliers, notably around down projections. Its first block rotation distributes extreme channels within a block. A zigzag permutation balances difficult channels across blocks, then another rotation smooths the new blocks. Permutation preserves values exactly and is cheap to fold into weights; the online transforms still need an implementation. The method adds structure guided by observed outliers rather than assuming a single random rotation will balance all regions. [33]

FlatQuant generalizes beyond diagonal scales and orthogonal rotations to learned invertible affine transforms around each layer. For a transform PPP, the algebraic identity is (XP)(P−1W)=XW(XP)(P^{-1}W)=XW(XP)(P−1W)=XW. A well-chosen nonorthogonal transform can flatten both operands more flexibly, but the inverse can amplify error if poorly conditioned. A dense online transform would defeat the inference goal. FlatQuant factorizes the transform with Kronecker structure and fuses the transform/quantization operations. Its quality and speed claims therefore describe the combined calibration and fused-kernel design, not an arbitrary dense matrix inserted into every layer. [34]

A Kronecker transform P=A⊗BP=A\otimes BP=A⊗B can act on a reshaped vector using two smaller matrix multiplies. If d=d1d2d=d_1d_2d=d1​d2​, its work is roughly O(d(d1+d2))O(d(d_1+d_2))O(d(d1​+d2​)) instead of O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2). Choosing balanced dimensions makes it practical, but the cost remains shape dependent. This is the central tension in increasingly expressive transformations: better quantized geometry can cost more online arithmetic, extra synchronization or a less regular packing layout.

The 2026 format-aware branch: DuQuant++ and mixed precision

Core idea. DuQuant++ aligns its outlier redistribution with the actual MXFP4 scale group, removing transformations that its group-local objective no longer needs. This makes the quantization recipe depend on the hardware format’s scale geometry rather than on bit width alone.

Microscaling changes the optimization boundary. Under MXFP4, every 32 values have an independent scale, so an outlier harms its local group rather than an entire token. DuQuant++ aligns an outlier-aware rotation with that 32-value group and removes the original cross-block permutation/second rotation. Its technical report argues that redistributing extremes between already independently scaled groups is unnecessary for this objective. The transferable lesson is to optimize the distribution inside the actual hardware scale group. The claim is conditional on the MXFP4 representation and the evaluated LLaMA-3 settings. [35]

SignRoundV2 takes another route: estimate the sensitivity of a layer from quantization-induced activation changes and loss-gradient information, then allocate bits under a budget before tuning. This is not equivalent to protecting layers with the largest weight norm. The useful unit of comparison is a model's average encoded bits and total kernel mix. A model with selected layers in eight bits can be better and faster than a uniform two-bit model, but a table that labels both simply “2 bit” conceals the decision. [30]

Derivation: an orthogonal change of basis preserves some operations, not all

Let R be orthogonal, RᵀR=I, and represent hidden state x as x′=Rx. A linear map y=Wx is preserved in the rotated basis by W′=RWRᵀ: W′x′=RWRᵀRx=RWx=Ry. For maps between different spaces use the appropriate input/output rotations. Residual addition commutes with R because R(x+f(x))=Rx+Rf(x).

RMS normalization without a learned elementwise gain is x/√(∥x∥²/d+ε). Orthogonality preserves ∥Rx∥²=∥x∥², so RMSNorm(Rx)=R·RMSNorm(x). A learned diagonal gain Γ generally does not commute with R: ΓR≠RΓ. It must be folded into neighboring linear maps or transformed consistently. LayerNorm also subtracts a coordinate mean, so arbitrary rotations need not commute with it unless the all-ones direction and relevant affine terms are handled.

The critical failure is elementwise nonlinearity. In general φ(Rx)≠Rφ(x). For ReLU, choose x=(1,−1) and the normalized two-dimensional Hadamard R:

Rx=(0,2),ReLU⁡(Rx)=(0,2),RReLU⁡(x)=R(1,0)=(12,12).\begin{aligned}Rx&=(0,\sqrt2),&\operatorname{ReLU}(Rx)&=(0,\sqrt2),\\R\operatorname{ReLU}(x)&=R(1,0)=\left(\frac1{\sqrt2},\frac1{\sqrt2}\right).\end{aligned}RxRReLU(x)​=(0,2​),=R(1,0)=(2​1​,2​1​).​ReLU(Rx)=(0,2​),

The two outputs differ. A function-preserving rotated FFN therefore folds transformations only across compatible linear/normalization boundaries and introduces paired online transforms where necessary. A transform cannot be pushed through a gate simply because it is orthogonal.

Why can rotation help after rounding? Before quantization, it preserves lengths and exact dot products. After scalar quantization, the coordinate grid is not rotation-invariant. Spreading one extreme coordinate over many coordinates can reduce the common quantization step and worst coordinate error. This is a statement about the interaction between basis and grid; random rotations are not guaranteed to produce identical downstream accuracy, and structured transforms trade theory, cost and distributional behavior.

Exercise — A dot product in two bases

Let x=(3,1), y=(2,−2), and R=(1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]]. Verify dot-product preservation. Would rounding each rotated coordinate to an integer preserve it exactly?

Show worked solution

xᵀy=6−2=4. Rx=(2√2,√2), Ry=(0,2√2), whose dot product is 0+4=4. Integer-rounded rotated vectors are (3,1) and (0,3), with dot product 3. The exact transform is invariant; the coordinatewise rounding operation is not. This example does not show that rotation is generally worse—it demonstrates why its benefit must be analyzed after quantization.

Derivation: stochastic rounding removes local bias, not total training error

Let a≤x≤a+Δ be adjacent representable values. Stochastic rounding returns a+Δ with probability p=(x−a)/Δ and a otherwise. Its expectation and conditional error variance can be computed exactly:

E[x^∣x]=p(a+Δ)+(1−p)a=a+pΔ=x,Var⁡(x^−x∣x)=p(1−p)Δ2≤Δ24.\begin{aligned}\mathbb E[\widehat x\mid x]&=p(a+\Delta)+(1-p)a=a+p\Delta=x,\\\operatorname{Var}(\widehat x-x\mid x)&=p(1-p)\Delta^2\le\frac{\Delta^2}{4}.\end{aligned}E[x∣x]Var(x−x∣x)​=p(a+Δ)+(1−p)a=a+pΔ=x,=p(1−p)Δ2≤4Δ2​.​

Nearest rounding has smaller worst-case absolute error inside a bin, but it can repeatedly erase a small update with the same sign. In stochastic rounding, an update below one representable step can still move the stored value with a proportional probability. Over repeated independent trials, the expected accumulated displacement can track the intended small movement.

Three limits matter. First, clipping outside the representable interval breaks this unbiasedness unless overflow is handled separately. Second, conditional unbiased rounding does not make a nonlinear network's output unbiased: generally E[f(x̂)]≠f(E[x̂]). A second-order expansion adds approximately ½tr(Hf Cov(x̂)) to the mean. Third, training trajectories use future gradients evaluated at earlier rounded parameters; local unbiasedness alone is not a proof of convergence or identical final quality.

This explains the role of stochastic rounding in low-precision training without assigning it magical exactness. Higher-precision master weights preserve small updates deterministically in another representation; stochastic rounding changes how updates cross a coarse grid. They are different mechanisms and can be combined with scale updates and protected operations.

3.8 The training branch: frozen bases, fake quantization, and native FP4 arithmetic

Problems and objectives. Post-training reconstruction has limits, and some goals require adaptation or learning under quantization noise. This parallel branch distinguishes training adapters over a frozen compressed base, updating model weights with simulated quantization, and performing forward/backward arithmetic in native low precision.

QLoRA: memory-efficient adaptation of a frozen model

Core idea. Freeze an NF4-compressed base model and train small low-rank adapters while reconstructing base weights for computation. The memory saving comes from compact base storage and avoiding base-weight optimizer states, not from training every operation in four-bit arithmetic.

QLoRA stores a frozen base in NF4, reconstructs weights for higher-precision computation, and trains low-rank adapters. With W^\hat WW^ frozen and ΔW=BA\Delta W=BAΔW=BA, the forward function is XW^+XBAX\hat W+XBAXW^+XBA. Gradients pass through the base's computation to earlier adapters, but no base-weight optimizer state is needed. This distinction is easy to miss: “frozen” does not mean the base layers are absent from backpropagation. [5]

Read the figure. Full fine-tuning has optimizer state tied to the whole model. LoRA shrinks the trainable portion; QLoRA additionally shrinks base-weight storage. Green arrows mark gradient flow, blue arrows parameter updates, and the paging route addresses memory spikes. NF4 and double quantization reduce persistent storage, whereas paged optimizers address the timing of memory demand. These are three separate contributions.

NF4 assigns nonuniform scalar representatives suited to a approximately normal weight distribution after block normalization; it is a lookup code, not an exponent/mantissa format. Double quantization compresses the block constants themselves, saving about 0.37 bits/parameter in the paper's setting. The datatype atlas derives the remaining metadata rather than rounding the answer down to four bits. Paged optimizer state can spill through unified memory when pressure rises; this does not make transfer free or guarantee all training runs become faster.

The final adapter must be evaluated under its serving representation. Merging BABABA into a dequantized base and requantizing changes the numerical model; serving separate adapters adds another operation. QLoRA's fine-tuning result is evidence about the frozen quantized base plus its adaptation procedure, not a claim that every NF4 checkpoint has an efficient integer inference kernel.

LLM-QAT and BitNet: what actually gets trained?

Core idea. LLM-QAT adapts a pretrained model through quantization-aware distillation using teacher-generated data, whereas BitNet learns with strongly constrained low-bit weights as part of training. They address different starting points and should not be treated as interchangeable checkpoint-conversion methods.

LLM-QAT starts from a pretrained model, generates calibration/training text from that model, and uses quantization-aware distillation to adapt weights under simulated low-bit weights, activations and KV. Sampling generated sequences maintains more diversity than repeatedly taking the teacher's highest-probability token. The teacher distribution provides the target rather than requiring original pretraining labels. Straight-through gradient estimates make the nondifferentiable rounding operation trainable in practice, but are surrogate gradients, not derivatives of exact integer rounding. [13]

QAT can compensate errors beyond a local layer-MSE objective, at the cost of data generation, optimization and potential distribution shift. It should report which parameters move, what data are used, which tensors are fake-quantized, and whether the tested runtime implements the same quantizer. Fake-quantized evaluation runs floating arithmetic on rounded values; it measures a numerical model, not automatically the latency of a packed low-bit implementation.

BitNet b1.58 takes a different starting point: linear weights are trained to use ternary values {−1,0,+1}\{-1,0,+1\}{−1,0,+1}, with normalization/scaling and quantized activations. A real-valued latent weight state receives training updates, while the forward calculation uses its ternary projection. The log⁡23≈1.585\log_2 3\approx1.585log2​3≈1.585 figure is the information content per ternary symbol. Straight two-bit packing costs two bits; denser groups, scales and nonternary tensors change the actual average. This is a native low-bit model design, not a drop-in PTQ conversion of an arbitrary pretrained BF16 checkpoint. [20]

NVFP4 pretraining: consistent forward/backward quantization

Core idea. Combine block-scaled FP4 operands with carefully chosen higher-precision operations, transforms, and rounding rules in the forward/backward recipe. The question is whether training converges comparably under this coordinated numerical design, rather than whether every tensor can be blindly cast to FP4.

The 2025 NVFP4 report studies a 12B hybrid Mamba–Transformer trained on 10T tokens. It combines E2M1 operands, hierarchical block scaling, selected high-precision layers, randomized Hadamards, and stochastic rounding. The reported validation/downstream agreement is with an FP8 training baseline under that recipe; evaluations are performed in BF16. It is therefore evidence for the training algorithm's convergence, not an isolated demonstration of FP4 inference quality or an end-to-end speed benchmark. [36]

Why does transpose consistency matter? For Y=XWY=XWY=XW, backpropagation uses dX=dYW⊤dX=dY W^\top dX=dYW⊤ and dW=X⊤dYdW=X^\top dYdW=X⊤dY. Quantizing W independently along two different one-dimensional grouping axes generally yields Qcol(W)≠Qrow(W)Q_{\mathrm{col}}(W)\ne Q_{\mathrm{row}}(W)Qcol​(W)=Qrow​(W). Then the backward multiplication uses a different effective weight matrix from the forward computation. The report uses shared 16×16 weight scales so the quantized representation is consistent across orientations; activation and gradient operands retain finer 1×16 scaling. Those shared scale values are replicated into hardware-facing per-16 scale slots, which is why unique scale count and actual operand storage differ in §4.4.

For weight-gradient GEMMs, transform both activation and output-gradient operands along their common reduction dimension. If R⊤R=IR^\top R=IR⊤R=I, (RX)⊤(RdY)=X⊤dY(RX)^\top (RdY)=X^\top dY(RX)⊤(RdY)=X⊤dY before rounding. This spreads block-level outliers without altering the exact product. The report uses randomized 16×16 Hadamards for this path; indiscriminately rotating every GEMM would add cost and can create inconsistent quantized weights. [36]

Read the figure. The main curve is training loss against trillions of tokens. Ablations branch from a shared NVFP4 checkpoint at about 3.43T tokens, so these are continuation experiments rather than independent complete retrainings. The inset defines relative difference as FP8−experimentFP8\frac{\mathrm{FP8}-\mathrm{experiment}}{\mathrm{FP8}}FP8FP8−experiment​: a more negative value means a worse loss than the FP8 reference. Removing stochastic rounding or the weight-gradient Hadamard visibly worsens this continuation. A smaller separation for another component does not prove it is irrelevant at all scales.

Stochastic rounding to adjacent representable levels a≤x≤ba\le x\le ba≤x≤b chooses bbb with probability x−ab−a\frac{x-a}{b-a}b−ax−a​ and aaa otherwise, making the conditional expectation equal to x when no clipping occurs. It reduces systematic gradient rounding bias but adds variance and does not fix saturation. In this recipe it is applied to gradients; weights and activations use nearest rounding. Master weights, accumulated weight gradients and optimizer state remain FP32, and attention/norm/nonlinear operations retain higher precision. “FP4 training” therefore describes selected GEMM operands, not four-bit optimizer memory or four-bit arithmetic everywhere.

The common thread from QLoRA to NVFP4 is to state exactly what is stored, what is multiplied, what is accumulated, and what is updated. These four answers often have different precisions. A convincing result connects the numerical recipe to its actual execution path and checks the tasks or training horizon that motivate using it.

Derivation: a continuous model for sensitivity-aware bit allocation

Partition a model into groups j containing nj scalar values. Suppose a high-resolution approximation predicts output distortion Dj(bj)=cj·2^(−2bj), where cj includes range, input sensitivity and group size. Minimize total distortion subject to a payload-bit budget B. For this derivation ignore integer bit widths, format restrictions and metadata, then add them back when interpreting the result.

min⁡{bj}∑jcj2−2bjsubject to ∑jnjbj=B,L=∑jcj2−2bj+λ ⁣(∑jnjbj−B),∂L∂bj=−2ln⁡(2)cj2−2bj+λnj=0,bj=12log⁡2 ⁣(2ln⁡(2)cjλnj).\begin{aligned}\min_{\{b_j\}}\quad&\sum_jc_j2^{-2b_j}\quad\text{subject to }\sum_jn_jb_j=B,\\\mathcal L&=\sum_jc_j2^{-2b_j}+\lambda\!\left(\sum_jn_jb_j-B\right),\\\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial b_j}&=-2\ln(2)c_j2^{-2b_j}+\lambda n_j=0,\\b_j&=\frac12\log_2\!\left(\frac{2\ln(2)c_j}{\lambda n_j}\right).\end{aligned}{bj​}min​L∂bj​∂L​bj​​j∑​cj​2−2bj​subject to j∑​nj​bj​=B,=j∑​cj​2−2bj​+λ(j∑​nj​bj​−B),=−2ln(2)cj​2−2bj​+λnj​=0,=21​log2​(λnj​2ln(2)cj​​).​

At the optimum, the marginal error reduction per extra stored bit is equal across unconstrained groups. Subtracting two conditions removes λ:

bj−bk=12log⁡2 ⁣(cj/njck/nk).b_j-b_k=\frac12\log_2\!\left(\frac{c_j/n_j}{c_k/n_k}\right).bj​−bk​=21​log2​(ck​/nk​cj​/nj​​).

A group with four times the sensitivity per scalar receives one additional bit in this ideal model. If a proposed width falls below a minimum or above a maximum, clamp it and solve for λ over the remaining free groups. This is a water-filling-like allocation in log distortion, derived from the assumed rate curve rather than a rule to “always keep the first layer at high precision.”

Hardware-supported choices are discrete, and scales/outlier streams add non-payload costs. An executable allocation can instead choose among candidate formats with measured error and byte cost, forming a multiple-choice knapsack problem. Kernel launch and mixed-format dispatch costs can also make an apparently superior memory/error allocation slower. The continuous solution is useful for understanding marginal tradeoffs and initializing a search; it is not an exact solution to mixed-precision deployment.

Exercise — One group is four times more sensitive

Two equally sized groups have c₁=4c₂ and an average budget of three bits per scalar. Solve the unconstrained continuous allocation. Which two integer widths realize it?

Show worked solution

b₁−b₂=½log₂4=1 and (b₁+b₂)/2=3, giving b₁=3.5 and b₂=2.5. No single pair of integer widths with this mean reproduces that exact optimum: (4,2) and (3,3) are candidates. Set c₂=1. Their distortions are 4/256+1/16=0.078125 and 4/64+1/64=0.078125, equal in this particular model; the continuous optimum gives 4/128+1/32=0.0625. Metadata and available kernels decide among executable choices. The tempting answer “4 and 2 are exact” misses the relaxation gap.

4A field guide to numeric formats and real bit costs

Keep three levels separate: a value code (such as E2M1), a scaling recipe (such as MXFP4), and a file/tensor encoding (such as GGUF Q4_K). A method such as AWQ can choose the values for a format; W4A16 only names operand widths.

4.1 From FP32 to FP4: what the bits mean

For a binary float, S/E/M counts sign, stored exponent, and stored fraction bits. A normal value is approximately (−1)S×2E−bias×(1.fraction)(-1)^S\times2^{E-\mathrm{bias}}\times(1.\mathrm{fraction})(−1)S×2E−bias×(1.fraction). More exponent bits buy range; more fraction bits buy spacing/precision near a given magnitude. Subnormals, reserved codes, and overflow rules depend on the particular format. The exponent and fraction counts describe the value code; they do not include any shared scale. [24]

Value formatS/E/M bitsStored bits/valueLargest finite magnitudeInterpretation
FP32 (binary32)1 / 8 / 2332≈3.40×10³⁸Broad range and fine precision; common reference/accumulator format.
TF321 / 8 / 10 nominal fraction bits for multiplication32 in memoryFP32-like rangeReduced-precision compute path; do not budget it as a 19-bit checkpoint.
FP16 (binary16)1 / 5 / 101665,504Finer spacing than BF16 near 1; narrower dynamic range.
BF161 / 8 / 716≈3.39×10³⁸FP32-like exponent range; coarser spacing than FP16.
FP8 E4M31 / 4 / 38448More precision than E5M2; the common finite-only E4M3 variant has NaN but no infinity.
FP8 E5M21 / 5 / 2857,344More range, coarser precision; supports infinity and NaN.
FP6 E3M2 / E2M31 / 3 / 2 or 1 / 2 / 36, packed28 / 7.5Two MX element choices trading range for spacing.
FP4 E2M11 / 2 / 14, packed6 before scalingPositive levels are 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6; signs supply negatives.

For normal values, the exponent biases are 127 for FP32/BF16/TF32, 15 for FP16/E5M2, 7 for E4M3, 3 for E3M2, and 1 for E2M3/E2M1. Adjacent normal values around 1 differ by approximately 2−M2^{-M}2−M: FP16 has 2−102^{-10}2−10 spacing, BF16 2−72^{-7}2−7. For example, E2M1 0 | 01 | 1 encodes +1.5+1.5+1.5. OCP FP4 and FP6 have no infinity/NaN codes; E4M3's special-value behavior differs from E5M2's. [18] [25]

FP32, FP16, and BF16 normally have no scale metadata: their effective element size is 32, 16, or 16 bits. TF32 is especially easy to misread: its multiply uses fewer meaningful fraction bits, while operands still occupy 32-bit storage. The FP8 values above describe the OCP/NVIDIA E4M3 and E5M2 encodings; names such as E4M3FN make the finite-only variant explicit. INT8/INT4 instead use an integer code plus an external scale; NF4 uses an index into a nonuniform 16-value table. [24] [25] [18]

Read the table. These are encodings, not empirical model results. E4M3 reuses almost all of its largest-exponent codes for finite values and reserves a NaN pattern; E5M2 retains infinity and NaN encodings. The table distinguishes smallest normal and smallest subnormal values. An E4M3 code has minimum positive normal 2−62^{-6}2−6 and subnormal 2−92^{-9}2−9; E5M2 has 2−142^{-14}2−14 and 2−162^{-16}2−16. Thus equal eight-bit storage does not imply equal overflow or underflow behavior. [37]

For a normal binary value with fraction integer fff and MMM fraction bits, use x=(−1)s2e−bias(1+f2M)x=(-1)^s2^{e-\mathrm{bias}}\left(1+\frac f{2^M}\right)x=(−1)s2e−bias(1+2Mf​). With an all-zero exponent and a nonzero subnormal fraction, the leading one disappears: x=(−1)s21−biasf2Mx=(-1)^s2^{1-\mathrm{bias}}\frac f{2^M}x=(−1)s21−bias2Mf​. The special treatment of the maximum exponent then follows the particular specification. These formulas explain why BF16 has fewer representable steps near one than FP16 despite the same element width. Conversion may also flush subnormals, saturate overflow, or propagate NaNs differently in a particular instruction; those semantics belong to the executed kernel.

Do not infer an encoding solely from E4M3. Variants with different biases, finite-only rules, or unsigned-zero conventions exist. The common E4M3FN described here is not automatically bit-compatible with every format carrying the same exponent/fraction counts. Similarly, TF32 describes reduced-precision multiplication of FP32-resident operands; its nominal 10 stored fraction bits of multiplication precision do not create a compact 19-bit model file. Accumulation precision is a separate field in any reliable numerical specification.

Derivation: exponent bits buy range, fraction bits buy relative resolution

For a binary normal floating-point value with sign s, unbiased exponent e, and m stored fraction bits, write x=(−1)ˢ·2ᵉ(1+f/2ᵐ), where f is an integer from zero to 2ᵐ−1. At a fixed exponent, adjacent representable values are separated by Δ=2^(e−m). Round-to-nearest gives absolute error at most Δ/2 in the interior of that binade.

∣x^−x∣≤2e−m−1,∣x∣≥2e⟹∣x^−x∣∣x∣≤2−m−1.\begin{aligned}|\widehat x-x|&\le2^{e-m-1},\\|x|\ge2^e\quad&\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{|\widehat x-x|}{|x|}\le2^{-m-1}.\end{aligned}∣x−x∣∣x∣≥2e​≤2e−m−1,⟹∣x∣∣x−x∣​≤2−m−1.​

The bound is the familiar unit-roundoff scale for normal values, not a bound across overflow or underflow. Subnormals use a fixed spacing tied to the minimum exponent and no implicit leading one. The normal-range relative-error bound no longer holds: sufficiently small nonzero inputs round to zero with 100% relative error, while absolute error stays at most half the subnormal spacing under nearest rounding with gradual underflow. NaNs, infinities and finite-only encodings also change which exponent/fraction codes are available; “E4M3” alone must be tied to the exact format convention in the atlas.

More exponent bits expand the available binades; more fraction bits subdivide each binade. BF16 and FP16 therefore solve different range–precision problems despite both occupying two bytes. A tensor scale multiplies all values and moves them between binades, helping avoid overflow or underflow. It does not create additional fraction bits within a normal binade.

A power-of-two shared scale changes an exponent exactly when representable, while an FP8 scale can introduce its own rounding. For reconstructed x̂=ŝq̂, expand the error around ideal s and q:

x^−sq=(s^−s)q+s(q^−q)+(s^−s)(q^−q).\widehat x-sq=(\widehat s-s)q+s(\widehat q-q)+(\widehat s-s)(\widehat q-q).x−sq=(s−s)q+s(q​−q)+(s−s)(q​−q).

Thus block-scale error is shared across the group's values. The cross term is often small but not identically zero. Counting scale bytes is necessary for memory accounting; analyzing scale error is separately necessary for numerical accuracy.

Exercise — Compare FP16 and BF16 within the normal range

Using m=10 for FP16 and m=7 for BF16, derive their round-to-nearest relative-error bounds for normal inputs. Does this establish which one is safer for gradients of unknown magnitude?

Show worked solution

FP16 gives 2⁻¹¹≈4.8828×10⁻⁴; BF16 gives 2⁻⁸=0.00390625, eight times larger. This comparison alone does not determine safety: FP16's smaller exponent range can overflow or underflow values that BF16 represents normally. A normal-range relative-error bound cannot be applied to a value outside that range.

4.2 The general storage equation

Let a tensor contain NNN logical values, each with a bbb-bit code. A group of GGG values has an sss-bit scale and, if needed, a zzz-bit zero point. Let TTT be tensor-level metadata bits. With dense bit packing and no row-specific padding, the exact byte-rounded budget is:

C=⌈NG⌉groups,B=⌈bN8⌉+C⌈s+z8⌉+⌈T8⌉bytes,when each group’s metadata is byte-rounded,beffective=8BN.Ideal bit-packed large-N limit:b+s+zG+TN.\begin{aligned}C&=\left\lceil\frac NG\right\rceil\quad\text{groups},\\B&=\left\lceil\frac{bN}{8}\right\rceil+C\left\lceil\frac{s+z}{8}\right\rceil+\left\lceil\frac T8\right\rceil\quad\text{bytes},\\&\text{when each group's metadata is byte-rounded},\\b_{\mathrm{effective}}&=\frac{8B}{N}.\\[6pt]\text{Ideal bit-packed large-$N$ limit:}\quad&b+\frac{s+z}{G}+\frac TN.\end{aligned}CBbeffective​Ideal bit-packed large-N limit:​=⌈GN​⌉groups,=⌈8bN​⌉+C⌈8s+z​⌉+⌈8T​⌉bytes,when each group’s metadata is byte-rounded,=N8B​.b+Gs+z​+NT​.​

For a fixed packed block containing nnn values in hhh bytes, use B=⌈Nn⌉hB=\left\lceil\frac Nn\right\rceil hB=⌈nN​⌉h and beffective=8⌈N/n⌉hNb_{\mathrm{effective}}=\frac{8\lceil N/n\rceil h}Nbeffective​=N8⌈N/n⌉h​; if rows are separately blocked, sum that expression over rows. For several precision levels, count the groups at each level. Alignment, transposed copies, outlier indices, file headers, and unquantized tensors add further bytes.

Btotal=∑t[Bcodes,t+∑ℓBscales,t,ℓ+Bzero,t+Bexceptions,t+Bpadding,t]+Bfile metadata,bmodel=8Btotal∑tNt.\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{total}}={}&\sum_t\left[B_{\mathrm{codes},t}+\sum_\ell B_{\mathrm{scales},t,\ell}\right.\\&\qquad\left.+B_{\mathrm{zero},t}+B_{\mathrm{exceptions},t}+B_{\mathrm{padding},t}\right]\\&+B_{\mathrm{file\ metadata}},\\b_{\mathrm{model}}={}&\frac{8B_{\mathrm{total}}}{\sum_tN_t}.\end{aligned}Btotal​=bmodel​=​t∑​[Bcodes,t​+ℓ∑​Bscales,t,ℓ​+Bzero,t​+Bexceptions,t​+Bpadding,t​]+Bfile metadata​,∑t​Nt​8Btotal​​.​

Worked example: one FP16 scale for every 128 FP8 values costs 8+16/128=8.1258+16/128 = 8.1258+16/128=8.125 bits/value when groups are full, not 8.128. For an NNN-value tensor, the exact packed budget is B=N+2⌈N128⌉B=N+2\left\lceil\frac N{128}\right\rceilB=N+2⌈128N​⌉ bytes (FP8 codes already occupy whole bytes). If N=129N=129N=129, two scales give 8×133/129≈8.2488\times 133/129\approx 8.2488×133/129≈8.248 bits/logical value. The last group's unused capacity matters at small or awkward sizes.

Two different denominators

Block bits/value divides a block's bytes by its block length. Model bits/parameter divides all stored tensor and metadata bytes by all model parameters. A GGUF model named Q4_K_M can exceed the 4.5 bits/value of a pure Q4_K tensor because it mixes tensor types. Peak GPU memory also includes runtime buffers and KV cache.

4.3 Eight- and six-bit recipes: the scale is part of the format

E8M0 means an eight-bit exponent-only shared scale, representing powers of two; it is not an ordinary E4M3 data value. OCP MX uses 32-value blocks for MXFP8, MXFP6, MXFP4, and MXINT8. A vendor's “FP8 block scaling” can use different scale precision and group geometry, as the FP32/128 example shows. For non-full blocks, use the exact formula in §4.2 and the runtime's padding rules. [18] [27]

Scale codes have their own edge cases. OCP E8M0 stores an unsigned biased exponent: byte u∈[0,254]u\in[0,254]u∈[0,254] represents 2u−1272^{u-127}2u−127, while 255 represents NaN. It has no zero or infinity code. An all-zero MX block represents zero through zero element codes and an appropriate finite scale. Multiplying by a power of two primarily shifts an exponent; E4M3 block scales have additional fractional resolution but more complex arithmetic. OCP defines the representation and dot-product semantics without mandating one universal algorithm for selecting a block's scale. [18]

For a blocked dot product, the mathematical operation is ∑gsA,gsB,g∑i∈gpA,ipB,i\sum_gs_{A,g}s_{B,g}\sum_{i\in g}p_{A,i}p_{B,i}∑g​sA,g​sB,g​∑i∈g​pA,i​pB,i​. Scale products occur for each block's partial sum. This is why microscaling can work efficiently on matrix hardware designed for it and why merely storing a 17-byte MXFP4 block does not establish that an older GPU has native MXFP4 arithmetic. The scale direction must also agree with the GEMM reduction dimension.

NF4 is a lookup codebook based on normal-distribution quantiles, including a zero code. Exact NVFP4 2D accounting: information versus an executable operand

For R×CR\times CR×C weights, shared 16×16 scaling has ⌈R16⌉⌈C16⌉\left\lceil\frac R{16}\right\rceil\left\lceil\frac C{16}\right\rceil⌈16R​⌉⌈16C​⌉ distinct scale values if tail tiles are supported. Deduplicating those values in an ideal serialized representation yields 4+8256+32RC=4.03125+32RC4+\frac8{256}+\frac{32}{RC}=4.03125+\frac{32}{RC}4+2568​+RC32​=4.03125+RC32​ for full tiles. This is a logical information count. It is not the default byte count of a Transformer Engine GPU operand: the NVFP4 training report states that each tile's scale is replicated for its constituent 1×16 blocks when supplied to tensor cores. Transformer Engine documents a rowwise scale array of shape [R,C/16][R,C/16][R,C/16] and a columnwise array [C,R/16][C,R/16][C,R/16], with the first scale dimension padded to a multiple of 128 and the second to a multiple of four. Brow=⌈RC2⌉+A128(R) A4(C/16)+Bglobal,Bcol=⌈RC2⌉+A128(C) A4(R/16)+Bglobal,col,beffective,row=8BrowRC,Bboth=Brow+Bcol−Bactually shared metadata.\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{row}}&=\left\lceil\frac{RC}{2}\right\rceil+A_{128}(R)\,A_4(C/16)+B_{\mathrm{global}},\\B_{\mathrm{col}}&=\left\lceil\frac{RC}{2}\right\rceil+A_{128}(C)\,A_4(R/16)+B_{\mathrm{global,col}},\\b_{\mathrm{effective,row}}&=\frac{8B_{\mathrm{row}}}{RC},\\B_{\mathrm{both}}&=B_{\mathrm{row}}+B_{\mathrm{col}}-B_{\mathrm{actually\ shared\ metadata}}.\end{aligned}Brow​Bcol​beffective,row​Bboth​​=⌈2RC​⌉+A128​(R)A4​(C/16)+Bglobal​,=⌈2RC​⌉+A128​(C)A4​(R/16)+Bglobal,col​,=RC8Brow​​,=Brow​+Bcol​−Bactually shared metadata​.​

With large aligned matrices, one physical scale slot per sixteen codes approaches 4.54.54.5 bits/value plus tensor metadata even when many scale slots repeat the same 2D tile value. Keeping rowwise and columnwise copies can approach twice that storage. The 2D scheme primarily buys forward/backward consistency, not automatically a 4.03125-bit GPU footprint. [19] [36]

The standard hierarchical scale construction chooses a global multiplier approximately global amax448×6\frac{\mathrm{global\ amax}}{448\times6}448×6global amax​, then an E4M3 local scale approximating block amax6 global scale\frac{\mathrm{block\ amax}}{6\,\mathrm{global\ scale}}6global scaleblock amax​. This describes the reconstruction convention; some APIs store an inverse scale. Confusing scale and inverse-scale conventions causes both incorrect calculations and overflow. Zero blocks, scale rounding and clipping need explicit handling in a real implementation.
