The current ggml NVFP4 structure above contains four local scale bytes and no FP32 global field inside that block. Do not append a per-block four-byte global scale because a different library has a tensor-level scale; inspect that library's reconstruction and tensor metadata. Conversely, a block-only count does not establish the complete file or runtime footprint. Names can coincide across ecosystems while their containers and scale conventions differ.

The IQ1_S cost below log⁡23\log_2 3log2​3 does not violate information theory: its structured vector codebook does not encode every possible independent ternary vector. Information limits apply to the set of all sequences the representation must support. IQ grids constrain that set; TQ encodings represent ternary symbols with a different packing scheme. “Importance-aware” describes how codes are selected using calibration importance information, while the struct describes how the selected result is stored.

For a row-blocked matrix with each row length CCC divisible by block length nnn, the exact tensor payload is R(C/n)hR(C/n)hR(C/n)h. The expression R⌈Cn⌉hR\left\lceil\frac Cn\right\rceil hR⌈nC​⌉h is appropriate only if a format or loader explicitly pads incomplete blocks; many ggml quantized operations require row divisibility and reject an unsupported shape. Always divide physical bytes by the original logical RCRCRC when reporting effective bits. Strides and alignment must not silently change the denominator.

A generalized formula for codebooks, exceptions, and hierarchical scales

A vector code can have fewer index bits than the cost of its learned dictionary suggests. Suppose JJJ groups of ggg values use MMM codebooks, 2B2^B2B entries per codebook, and ccc bits per codebook scalar. With one shared set of books and dense bit-packed indices:

Bindices=⌈JMB8⌉,Bcodebooks=⌈M 2Bgc8⌉,Btotal=Bindices+Bcodebooks+Brow scales+Bother,beffective=8BtotalNlogical.\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{indices}}&=\left\lceil\frac{JMB}{8}\right\rceil,\\B_{\mathrm{codebooks}}&=\left\lceil\frac{M\,2^Bgc}{8}\right\rceil,\\B_{\mathrm{total}}&=B_{\mathrm{indices}}+B_{\mathrm{codebooks}}+B_{\mathrm{row\ scales}}+B_{\mathrm{other}},\\b_{\mathrm{effective}}&=\frac{8B_{\mathrm{total}}}{N_{\mathrm{logical}}}.\end{aligned}Bindices​Bcodebooks​Btotal​beffective​​=⌈8JMB​⌉,=⌈8M2Bgc​⌉,=Bindices​+Bcodebooks​+Brow scales​+Bother​,=Nlogical​8Btotal​​.​

AQLM's two eight-bit indices for each eight-value group give two index bits per scalar. With FP16 books the shared dictionary costs 2×256×8×2=81922\times 256\times 8\times 2=81922×256×8×2=8192 bytes; amortize it over the tensor, not over each group. For fixed implicit codebooks, serialized dictionary cost may be zero while the runtime still uses a lookup table. For multiple tensor-specific dictionaries, sum each separately. [12]

For hierarchical scale quantization, write J1=⌈NG1⌉J_1=\left\lceil\frac N{G_1}\right\rceilJ1​=⌈G1​N​⌉ and J2=⌈J1G2⌉J_2=\left\lceil\frac{J_1}{G_2}\right\rceilJ2​=⌈G2​J1​​⌉. Four-bit values with eight-bit first-level scales and FP32 second-level scales cost ⌈N2⌉+J1+4J2+Boffset\left\lceil\frac N2\right\rceil+J_1+4J_2+B_{\mathrm{offset}}⌈2N​⌉+J1​+4J2​+Boffset​ bytes under a packed-tail convention. Sparse exceptions additionally require their values, indices and pointers; keeping a BF16 residual window requires its full uncompressed payload. This single accounting framework covers NF4 double quantization, mixed precision, vector codes and KV windows without confusing a payload label with total storage.

Read any precision claim in three steps

Ask (1) what value code is used, (2) which scales/zero points and group shape are stored, and (3) which tensors remain in another type or need duplicate runtime layouts. Then calculate effective bits/value and separately measure peak memory and speed. W4A16, MXFP4, NVFP4, and Q4_K_M.gguf describe different parts of that answer.

Derivation: effective bits are a physical storage ledger

Let an R×C logical matrix use blocks of G values along each row. Each block stores G payload codes at b bits and h metadata bytes. Assume the format pads a last partial block to G values and each serialized block rounds to whole bytes. Then blocks per row are J=ceil(C/G), block bytes are H=ceil(Gb/8)+h, and tensor bytes before outer alignment are RJH. If each row stride is padded to an A-byte boundary, replace JH by A ceil(JH/A).

Bphysical=RA⌈⌈C/G⌉HA⌉+Btensor metadata,beffective=8BphysicalRC.\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{physical}}&=RA\left\lceil\frac{\lceil C/G\rceil H}{A}\right\rceil+B_{\mathrm{tensor\ metadata}},\\b_{\mathrm{effective}}&=\frac{8B_{\mathrm{physical}}}{RC}.\end{aligned}Bphysical​beffective​​=RA⌈A⌈C/G⌉H​⌉+Btensor metadata​,=RC8Bphysical​​.​

This expression counts actual padding; b+8h/G is only the full-group, unaligned asymptotic average. If a library forbids C not divisible by G, the ceil formula describes a hypothetical padded representation, not a supported operand. Distinguish a valid shape from an accounting convention.

With hierarchical scales, add each level once at its actual sharing granularity. With sparse exceptions, include values, indices, row pointers and padding. With a second transposed operand copy, add its separately rounded layout and subtract only metadata physically shared. A tensor-global scale's cost is divided by all logical elements, whereas repeated block scales are divided by their local group. Equal numerical scale values are not free unless the representation actually deduplicates them.

For an entire model, average by scalar count: bmodel=Σt Nt bt/Σt Nt for tensor payload/metadata accounted consistently. Averaging the per-tensor bit widths arithmetically gives small biases and huge matrices equal weight. Runtime memory adds other objects such as dequantization buffers and activations; those belong in a total footprint ledger rather than being silently attributed to the weight encoding.

Exercise — A small tensor with unexpectedly expensive four-bit storage

Assume a supported padded format with R=3, C=33, G=32, b=4, h=2 bytes per block and 16-byte aligned row strides. There are no tensor-global bytes. Compute the effective bits. Compare with its asymptotic 4.5-bit count.

Show worked solution

J=ceil(33/32)=2 blocks per row. H=16+2=18 bytes. Unaligned row bytes are 36, aligned to 48. Total is 3·48=144 bytes for 99 logical values, giving 1152/99≈11.6364 bits/value. Full groups without stride padding approach 4+16/32=4.5 bits. The small example is dominated by incomplete blocks and row alignment; it does not contradict the asymptotic formula.

5KV-cache quantization: the context multiplier

Problems and objectives. Unlike fixed weight storage, cache storage grows with context and concurrency and is appended during generation. The central problem is to choose quantization axes and recent-token handling that control attention error without making metadata or repeated requantization dominate the savings.

Weight size is fixed; KV size grows with every retained token and every live sequence.

For a decoder with LLL layers, HkvH_{\mathrm{kv}}Hkv​ key/value heads, head dimension ddd, context length TTT, and bbb bits per cached value, the ideal cache payload per sequence is:

BKV=2⏟K and V LHkvdT b8bytes, before scales/allocator overhead.B_{\mathrm{KV}}=\underbrace{2}_{\text{K and V}}\,LH_{\mathrm{kv}}dT\,\frac b8\quad\text{bytes, before scales/allocator overhead}.BKV​=K and V2​​LHkv​dT8b​bytes, before scales/allocator overhead.

Worked model: let L=32L=32L=32, Hkv=8H_{\mathrm{kv}}=8Hkv​=8, d=128d=128d=128, and T=8192T=8192T=8192. BF16 KV needs 2×32×8×128×8192×2=1,073,741,8242\times 32\times 8\times 128\times 8192\times 2 = 1,073,741,8242×32×8×128×8192×2=1,073,741,824 bytes, exactly 1 GiB per sequence. Ideal INT8 halves this to 0.5 GiB; ideal four-bit quarters it to 0.25 GiB. At 32 concurrent full-length sequences, BF16 KV alone would need 32 GiB. Real memory adds scales, padding, allocator blocks, and temporary unquantized tokens.

Quantizing weights does not shrink this cache. Thus a 4-bit model that fits on a device can still run out of memory at long context or high batch. Grouped-query attention reduces HkvH_{\mathrm{kv}}Hkv​ and combines multiplicatively with cache quantization; the formula makes their separate contributions clear.

Keys and values behave differently. KIVI reports that key distributions favor per-channel quantization while values favor per-token quantization, and uses a residual high-precision window for recent tokens. KVQuant also studies per-channel keys, quantization relative to rotary positional embeddings, nonuniform grids, and outlier handling. These are research observations, not a promise that every model tolerates two-bit KV. [6] [21]

KV error changes an attention computation, not just one stored number: quantized KKK perturbs scores QK⊤QK^\top QK⊤ and potentially which tokens receive probability mass; quantized VVV perturbs the weighted output. Evaluate cache precision at your actual context lengths, with retrieval and generation tests, and compare both quality and batch capacity.

5.1 KIVI and KVQuant: where the scales live

Core idea. KIVI uses per-channel keys, per-token values, and a recent full-precision window; KVQuant adds calibrated pre-RoPE key coding and sparse outlier protection. Both allocate precision around the way key and value errors enter attention, while making different streaming and metadata tradeoffs.

KIVI's observation: in its evaluated Llama-family caches, large key values tend to recur in fixed feature channels. A per-token key scale lets those channels consume resolution from ordinary channels. KIVI therefore groups keys across a chunk of token positions within each channel. Values lack the same persistent channel-outlier pattern; their effect is a probability-weighted sum over tokens, so KIVI groups value dimensions within each token. In its Llama-2-13B analysis, per-channel keys reduced its attention-score error measure from 47.00 to 9.60 versus per-token keys; per-token values reduced its attention-output error measure from 49.89 to 3.55 versus per-channel values. Those are the paper's internal error metrics, not percentage-point task improvements. [6]

The streaming detail: a key's per-channel scale cannot be finalized until a token chunk fills. KIVI keeps recent keys and values at full precision in a residual window, periodically quantizes old keys by channel/chunk, and appends older values in per-token groups. Attention combines quantized old cache with the recent window. The residual window adds memory but was important for harder generation tasks in the authors' tests. Report its size and the measured peak memory when claiming “2-bit KV.” [6]

KVQuant also treats keys and values according to their distributions. Its key path considers quantization before rotary position embedding, uses per-channel key grids, and isolates outliers; it fits nonuniform codebooks using sensitivity information. The goal is extreme context length at roughly three-bit KV precision in its reported setup. Those choices make conversion, attention-kernel integration, and actual model/position-encoding compatibility part of the comparison. [21]

Error path

A key perturbation changes softmax⁡(QK⊤/d)\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt d)softmax(QK⊤/d​), potentially selecting another token. A value perturbation changes the contents retrieved after the attention weights are chosen. This explains why one grouping axis need not be best for both caches, and why long-context retrieval tests are more informative than KV tensor MSE alone.

Read the figure. Prefill creates the cache in larger blocks. During decoding, the old quantized keys and the new high-precision residual keys produce separate score fragments which are concatenated in the correct token order. A fused mixed-precision multiplication consumes quantized old keys. The figure omits the value/output path for readability; both paths still exist. The residual region also delays per-channel scale selection until enough tokens have arrived. [6]

The residual window creates a context-dependent effective bit width. If TqT_qTq​ tokens are quantized at effective bqb_qbq​ bits/value and TrT_rTr​ remain at bhib_{\mathrm{hi}}bhi​, then bavg=Tqbq+TrbhiTq+Trb_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{T_qb_q+T_rb_{\mathrm{hi}}}{T_q+T_r}bavg​=Tq​+Tr​Tq​bq​+Tr​bhi​​ before page padding and allocator metadata. At short context, an FP16 window can dominate; at long context its fraction shrinks. A universal “8× smaller than FP16” claim for a two-bit payload ignores this lifecycle.

Read the figure. The first two surfaces compare keys from the same layer before and after RoPE; stable channel ridges become position-dependent mixtures after rotation. The third surface is values, with a different magnitude range and distribution. The axes identify channel, token and magnitude. This motivates both the per-channel key granularity and the choice to quantize before positional rotation; it does not say that RoPE is harmful to the original model. [21]

KVQuant combines pre-RoPE key quantization, sensitivity-weighted nonuniform scalar levels and per-vector sparse outliers. With a fixed calibration-derived per-channel scale, it avoids rescaling every earlier key when a new maximum arrives. Online value scales can be computed per token without changing previous tokens. The implementation must apply position information consistently during attention and include sparse lookups in its kernel cost. Its million-token cache-capacity estimates should not be read as proof that the underlying model solves million-token tasks accurately.

A first-order attention error decomposition is useful. Let p=softmax⁡(z)p=\operatorname{softmax}(z)p=softmax(z), z=qK⊤/dz=qK^\top/\sqrt dz=qK⊤/d​, and o=pVo=pVo=pV. Small perturbations give δo≈δpV+pδV\delta o\approx \delta p V+p \delta Vδo≈δpV+pδV, with δp=(diag⁡(p)−pp⊤)δz\delta p=(\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top)\delta zδp=(diag(p)−pp⊤)δz. A key error perturbs the allocation of probability among tokens; a value error perturbs what is retrieved. The influence depends on q, the probability distribution, and the value directions. This derives why minimizing independent KV MSE is only a proxy and why retrieval, arithmetic and multi-turn tests can react differently.

Recent work explores rotation and residual coding more directly. TurboQuant combines random rotation, scalar quantization and a one-bit residual correction designed for inner products; UltraQuant studies mapping rotated low-bit KV to hardware-native microscaling kernels. These families make the distinction between vector-reconstruction error, attention-score error and executable datatype particularly important. See the dedicated KV Cache guide for their algorithms, storage accounting and contextual benchmarks; neither removes the need to report protected layers, residual regions or the actual scale representation. [38] [39]

6When quantization wins in hardware

6.1 Two roofline sketches

For batch-one decode, assume a dense model has NNN parameters. A rough forward step performs ≈2N\approx 2N≈2N multiply/add FLOPs and streams NpNpNp weight bytes, where ppp is effective bytes per parameter. Ignoring KV and overhead, weight arithmetic intensity is ≈2/p\approx 2/p≈2/p FLOP/byte. BF16 gives about 111; an effective 4.1254.1254.125-bit format gives about 3.883.883.88. Shrinking weights can move this bandwidth floor substantially, but the limit is less impressive once KV reads and dequantization are included.

As batch grows, one weight read serves many tokens, so the weight-side intensity rises roughly with batch size until compute or KV traffic becomes limiting. This is why W4A16 can be excellent for small-batch decode but W8A8/FP8 may be preferable for large-batch prefill or throughput-oriented serving. A W4A8 kernel can target both terms if numerics and hardware cooperate; QQQ is one research example, not a universal performance ranking. [15]

6.2 Four costs that erase a theoretical gain

  1. Unpacking and scale application. Packed nibbles must be decoded; group scales need loads and multiplies. Fusing this into a matmul matters.
  2. Layout conversion. A checkpoint may be compact on disk but repacked or expanded at load time. Measure resident memory after warm-up, not only file size.
  3. Unsupported operations. Norms, softmax, routing, output sampling, and some attention paths may remain higher precision. W4A4 does not mean the entire transformer is four-bit.
  4. Hardware mismatch. A GPU can load a format without natively executing its advertised low-precision GEMM. Framework compatibility tables change; inspect the kernel path on the target device. [17] [19]
The measurement that decides

Benchmark time to first token, inter-token latency, total output tokens/s, and goodput under a latency target across prompt lengths and concurrency levels. Report the exact model, quantized tensors, scale group, kernel/backend, device, batch, and context. “2× smaller” is a storage result until these measurements establish a serving result.

6.3 A kernel case study: where W4A16 earns its speed

Core idea. Marlin organizes packed INT4 weights, scales, activation reuse, and pipelined dequantization around GPU matrix execution. Its contribution is converting compressed storage into useful W4A16 throughput, which the quantizer alone does not guarantee.

Marlin is a concrete example of designing the decode path around packed INT4 weights and FP16 inputs. It reuses activations through registers/cache, pipelines weight loads, lays out packed weights and scales for the intended tensor-core tile, and overlaps dequantization with matrix work. It also partitions work to keep SMs busy at moderate batch sizes. These are execution decisions; the quantizer can supply accurate codes without supplying any of them. [41]

The public Marlin comparison uses group 128 and explicitly counts 0.125 scale bits per weight, giving a storage ratio 16/4.125≈3.87916/4.125\approx 3.87916/4.125≈3.879. Its near-ideal speedups are measured for particular NVIDIA GPUs, matrix shapes and batch ranges. They are not a bound on complete model speed. KV traffic, attention, layer norms, sampling, network collectives and scale handling consume time outside that matrix benchmark. This is a good example of a performance claim whose denominator must be read carefully.

A useful latency model is t=max⁡ ⁣(weight bytesBW,matmul FLOPsFeff)+tunhiddent=\max\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{weight\ bytes}}{\mathrm{BW}},\frac{\mathrm{matmul\ FLOPs}}{F_{\mathrm{eff}}}\right)+t_{\mathrm{unhidden}}t=max(BWweight bytes​,Feff​matmul FLOPs​)+tunhidden​, with an additional KV term when attention competes for bandwidth. Quantization reduces the first term; native W8A8 or FP4 hardware can also reduce the second. Dequantization that overlaps perfectly may disappear from the critical path; a serial scale reduction or transpose does not. The strongest evidence is a profiler trace plus complete-model latency under representative concurrency, not the ratio of advertised tensor-core peaks.

Derivation: local reconstruction error can amplify through depth

Let the original model's layer maps be fℓ and the quantized maps be f̂ℓ. Define hℓ+1=fℓ(hℓ), ĥℓ+1=f̂ℓ(ĥℓ), and error eℓ=∥ĥℓ−hℓ∥. Assume fℓ is Lℓ-Lipschitz on the relevant region and the local discrepancy ∥f̂ℓ(u)−fℓ(u)∥≤εℓ holds at the actual quantized states u. Add and subtract fℓ(ĥℓ):

eℓ+1≤∥f^ℓ(h^ℓ)−fℓ(h^ℓ)∥+∥fℓ(h^ℓ)−fℓ(hℓ)∥≤εℓ+Lℓeℓ.e0=0⟹eL≤∑j=0L−1εj∏k=j+1L−1Lk.\begin{aligned}e_{\ell+1}&\le\lVert\widehat f_\ell(\widehat h_\ell)-f_\ell(\widehat h_\ell)\rVert+\lVert f_\ell(\widehat h_\ell)-f_\ell(h_\ell)\rVert\\&\le\varepsilon_\ell+L_\ell e_\ell.\\e_0=0\quad&\Longrightarrow\quad e_L\le\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\varepsilon_j\prod_{k=j+1}^{L-1}L_k.\end{aligned}eℓ+1​e0​=0​≤∥f​ℓ​(hℓ​)−fℓ​(hℓ​)∥+∥fℓ​(hℓ​)−fℓ​(hℓ​)∥≤εℓ​+Lℓ​eℓ​.⟹eL​≤j=0∑L−1​εj​k=j+1∏L−1​Lk​.​

An early perturbation can be amplified by all subsequent layers. If every Lℓ=1, the bound is Σ εℓ; if Lℓ>1 it can grow much faster. Residual maps f(x)=x+g(x) have the safe bound Lf≤1+Lg, though this can be very pessimistic because directions and cancellations are ignored.

This is a worst-case guarantee under strong local bounds, not a prediction of perplexity. Calibration normally measures average error on a finite set, so it has not established a uniform εℓ over every state the quantized network may visit. Distribution shift and errors changing later inputs create a gap between a good calibration reconstruction and good task performance.

If the final logit perturbation is bounded in infinity norm by εz, a greedy token with original winner margin greater than 2εz cannot change: its logit can fall by εz while the runner-up can rise by at most εz. Small-margin decisions can flip even under small tensor error. During autoregressive generation, one flipped token then changes all future inputs. Thus a low average perplexity change and bitwise identical output are very different contracts.

Exercise — Certify one greedy decision

Original top logits are 4.0 and 3.7. Every logit changes by at most 0.1. Is the greedy winner guaranteed stable? What if the bound is 0.2?

Show worked solution

The original margin is 0.3. With εz=0.1, 0.3>2εz=0.2, so the winner remains strictly ahead. With εz=0.2, the sufficient condition fails: the winner could fall to 3.8 and the runner-up rise to 3.9. Failure of the condition does not prove a flip; it means this bound cannot rule one out.

7A sound quantization workflow

Treat every candidate as a controlled experiment against the same full-precision baseline.

  1. Freeze the baseline. Record model revision, tokenizer, chat template, BF16/FP16 output quality, serving backend, hardware, prompt/output length distributions, batch/concurrency, and latency targets.
  2. State the bottleneck. Check weight memory, KV memory at target context, and prefill/decode utilization. This determines whether to try W4A16, W8A8/FP8, KV quantization, or a combination first.
  3. Choose representative calibration data. Include the languages, coding/math patterns, prompt lengths, and activation shapes expected in service. Keep an independent holdout set. Calibration can overfit: AWQ explicitly tests generalization across domains, while GPTQ and SmoothQuant use sampled activations for their reconstruction/scaling decisions. [2] [3] [4]
  4. Compare a small ladder. Start with BF16, a simple INT8/FP8 option, and one 4-bit weight-only option supported by your backend. Add finer groups, GPTQ/AWQ, or selective higher precision only if measured quality requires them. For long context, add a separate KV-precision sweep.
  5. Measure multiple kinds of quality. Use held-out perplexity or negative log-likelihood for broad regression, then task tests for reasoning, code, instruction following, multilingual text, structured output, and long-context retrieval. Check rare catastrophic failures, not just mean score. Keep decoding settings identical.
  6. Measure the actual deployment. Report checkpoint bytes, warm resident memory, peak memory under load, TTFT, TPOT, throughput, and quality deltas at each concurrency and context point. Re-run if a backend silently changes kernels or dequantizes to BF16.

The comparison should hold model, prompts, sampling settings, and evaluation harness fixed. Method papers use different models, calibration sets, GPUs, and baselines, so their speedup numbers cannot be ranked as if they came from one experiment. An independent study also found that compressed models can be slower despite lower memory use. [14]

8Decision guide

Your bottleneckFirst candidateWhat can reverse the choice
Model does not fit; low-batch local generationSupported W4A16 or GGUF 4/5-bit typeSmall models and sensitive tasks may prefer 5/8 bits; check kernel and effective bits/weight.
Compute-heavy prefill, large serving batchW8A8 INT8 or FP8 with native GEMMActivation outliers, unavailable hardware path, or accuracy failures; consider smoothing/rotations.
Long context or limited concurrency from KV memoryTry 8-bit KV, then lower precision if evaluated quality permitsAttention sensitivity, scale overhead, backend support, and recent-token residual policy.
Four-bit weights lose too much qualitySmaller groups; GPTQ/AWQ; mixed-precision sensitive layersMetadata, conversion time, and kernel support can consume savings.
Memory-limited adapter fine-tuningQLoRA/NF4Serving still needs its own format and benchmark after adapter integration.
Training a model from scratch for extreme compressionQAT or native low-bit architectureHigher training complexity and a specialized runtime; PTQ comparisons are not equivalent.

A reasonable default experiment for an unfamiliar model is BF16 versus a backend-supported W4A16 candidate plus an 8-bit W8A8/FP8 candidate, at real prompt lengths and batch sizes. Then test KV quantization independently if cache memory matters. This is a decision procedure, not a blanket recommendation for a particular method or device.

9What the results actually say

There is no one-dimensional winner. The tables below preserve each experiment's model, precision, and metric. Lower perplexity (PPL) is better; higher task accuracy is better.

9.0 How to read the comparisons as experiments

The following tables answer several different questions: whether a fixed model retains quality, whether a bigger quantized model beats a smaller uncompressed one at equal memory, and whether an executable recipe improves latency. Those are separate comparisons. A fair fixed-model accuracy experiment holds tokenizer, evaluation context, task prompting and checkpoint version constant. A fair deployment comparison may change model size or GPU count, but should then say that it measures an equal-budget system choice.

Quality metrics also have different units. Perplexity is exponentiated mean negative log likelihood, so two absolute perplexity differences are not automatically comparable across corpora. For perplexities P0,P1P_0,P_1P0​,P1​, the cross-entropy change is ln⁡(P1/P0)\ln(P_1/P_0)ln(P1​/P0​) nats/token. Task accuracy is typically a percentage; a drop from 60% to 58% is two percentage points, not two percent relative. A mean across tasks can hide a major failure on a smaller but crucial task. Report both aggregate and relevant per-task behavior.

The tables retain the source's contexts and tuning distinctions. Read “near baseline” as an empirical observation for those evaluations, not equality of logits or a guarantee of identical generated sequences. No experiments in this guide claim an independent reproduction of the paper results.

9.4 Independent comparison and a long-context stress test

PTQ-Bench evaluated representative methods under one benchmark implementation on Llama-3 8B. Its PPL is an average over language-modeling sets; accuracy is its mean over evaluated reasoning tasks. W4 and W3 are nominal weight precisions, so effective checkpoint sizes still need separate measurement. [22]

Method in PTQ-BenchW4 PPL ↓W4 accuracy ↑W3 PPL ↓W3 accuracy ↑
AWQ7.9861.23%9.8354.65%
GPTQ7.9660.77%10.8452.19%

Read the pattern: W4 AWQ and GPTQ are close and lead this particular study; AWQ leads its W3 accuracy. The striking OmniQuant W3 decline is a finding for this implementation, model, and setting, not a verdict on every OmniQuant recipe. At W2, the same study reports severe collapse for several of these implementations, which motivates purpose-built extreme-bit methods and model-specific validation. [22]

A separate EMNLP 2025 study tested 9,700 long-context examples across five Llama-3.1/Qwen-2.5 models and FP8, GPTQ-INT8, AWQ-INT4, GPTQ-INT4, and BNB-NF4. Its 8-bit variants averaged about a 0.8% accuracy drop, while some four-bit task/model combinations lost up to 59%, with larger problems on non-English inputs. That result is a reason to run the target task and context length even when short-text PPL looks close to FP16. It does not say every four-bit model suffers a 59% loss. [23]

9.5 KV results: the recent-token window matters

KIVI's Llama-2 generation results compare FP16 cache, fake two-bit quantization of every token using the better K-per-channel/V-per-token axes, and the actual two-bit KIVI scheme with a recent full-precision window. These are GSM8K accuracy percentages in the paper's evaluation. [6]

KV cacheLlama-2 7B GSM8K ↑Llama-2 13B GSM8K ↑
FP1613.50%22.67%
2-bit, every token quantized, K-channel/V-token5.76%12.21%

The residual window recovers much of the lost GSM8K accuracy in this test, at a memory cost. In the paper's Llama-2-7B LongBench table, mean score is 44.52 for FP16 KV and 44.27 for KIVI-2; individual tasks still vary. KIVI reports using up to 2.6× less peak memory including model weights and 2.35–3.47× more throughput from larger feasible batches under its workloads. Those system numbers should be remeasured with the intended cache length, batch, and backend. [6]

9.6 Which method to try for which constraint

ConstraintPromising familyObserved weakness / cost
Fast, simple baselineRTN with a supported 8-bit or 4-bit formatCan waste levels on salient channels; weak at extreme bits.
Weight-only 4-bit qualityAWQ or GPTQ, then compare on your dataPaper and benchmark gaps are often small; layout/kernel and calibration can decide.
Weight-only 3-bit qualityAWQ, GPTQ, or a combined/advanced recipeAccuracy loss widens; metadata and workload-specific failures matter more.
Compute-heavy W8A8SmoothQuant or native FP8 path; LLM.int8() if outliers remainFP16 outlier path and dynamic scaling have different kernel costs.
W4A4 or joint W/A/KVQuaRot/SpinQuant or learned block calibrationOnline transforms, offline optimization, and specialized kernels.
Near-two-bit weightsAQLM, QuIP#, SpQR, or QAT research pathQuality gap to FP16, expensive conversion, and narrower runtime support.
Long-context KV capacity8-bit cache first; KIVI/KVQuant for lower-bit researchAttention errors and recent-window/scale overhead.

These are starting hypotheses from the cited experiments, not a universal leaderboard. For a real choice, hold the base model, calibration sample, bit accounting, eval tasks, backend, hardware, context, and batch fixed; plot quality against peak memory and measured latency. A method that wins PPL by 0.01 may be a worse deployment if its kernel is much slower or it fails the user's key task. [14] [22]

10Open questions and boundaries

  • Extreme bits: Below four bits, the trade among calibration cost, codebook complexity, reconstruction quality, and fast kernels remains active. Research gains in one model family need replication elsewhere.
  • Joint precision allocation: The optimal bits for weights, activations, and KV cache vary by layer, head, token position, and workload. Flexible policies add metadata and scheduling complexity.
  • Long-context reliability: Tiny attention-score changes can move probability mass away from a needed distant token. Short-text perplexity misses this failure mode.
  • Evaluation beyond averages: Quantization can have uneven effects on rare tasks or languages; the right deployment threshold depends on the application, not one benchmark.
  • Portable kernels: MXFP4, NVFP4, INT4, GGUF types, and framework-specific packed formats are not interchangeable artifacts. Compatibility and conversion costs remain a systems problem.

ADerivations and accounting

A.1 Why activation-aware error has a Hessian-like matrix

Let W^=W+ΔW\hat W=W+\Delta WW^=W+ΔW and collect calibration inputs in rows of XXX. Then Y^−Y=XΔW\hat Y-Y=X\Delta WY^−Y=XΔW. Squared Frobenius reconstruction error is:

∥XΔW∥F2=tr⁡ ⁣((ΔW)TXTXΔW).\lVert X\Delta W\rVert_F^2=\operatorname{tr}\!\left((\Delta W)^{\mathsf T}X^{\mathsf T}X\Delta W\right).∥XΔW∥F2​=tr((ΔW)TXTXΔW).

Thus the input correlation matrix X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X weights error directions. A per-weight nearest rounding rule ignores that coupling; a compensation method can adjust other weights after quantizing one column. This is the intuition for GPTQ. It is a layer-output objective, not a proof of end-task accuracy. [2]

A.2 Why equivalent scaling preserves the original layer

For any invertible diagonal DDD, insert D−1D=ID^{-1}D=ID−1D=I: XW=(XD−1)(DW)XW=(XD^{-1})(DW)XW=(XD−1)(DW). Before rounding, outputs are identical. After rounding, the two operands have different numeric ranges; this is the opportunity exploited by SmoothQuant and related scaling schemes. It is crucial to transform the matching weight axis. [4]

A.3 A memory plan that keeps units honest

7B, BF16:7×109×2  B=14.0×109  B≈13.04  GiB,7B, ideal 4-bit:7×109×0.5  B=3.5×109  B≈3.26  GiB,16-bit scale/128:7×109×0.015625  B≈0.109×109  B,Illustrative total:3.609×109  B≈3.36  GiB.\begin{aligned}\text{7B, BF16:}\quad&7\times10^9\times2\;\mathrm B=14.0\times10^9\;\mathrm B\approx13.04\;\mathrm{GiB},\\\text{7B, ideal 4-bit:}\quad&7\times10^9\times0.5\;\mathrm B=3.5\times10^9\;\mathrm B\approx3.26\;\mathrm{GiB},\\\text{16-bit scale/128:}\quad&7\times10^9\times0.015625\;\mathrm B\approx0.109\times10^9\;\mathrm B,\\\text{Illustrative total:}\quad&3.609\times10^9\;\mathrm B\approx3.36\;\mathrm{GiB}.\end{aligned}7B, BF16:7B, ideal 4-bit:16-bit scale/128:Illustrative total:​7×109×2B=14.0×109B≈13.04GiB,7×109×0.5B=3.5×109B≈3.26GiB,7×109×0.015625B≈0.109×109B,3.609×109B≈3.36GiB.​

This calculation assumes every parameter is in an identical group format and excludes zero points, exceptions, higher-precision tensors, KV cache, and runtime memory. A “70B in 35 GB” headline is similarly an ideal weight payload, not a complete capacity plan.

A.4 Why weight-only intensity rises with batching

One decode step for BBB sequences uses roughly 2BN2BN2BN weight-related FLOPs while ideally reading the same NpNpNp weight bytes once. So weight-side arithmetic intensity is 2B/p2B/p2B/p. The approximation breaks when cache traffic, activation traffic, insufficient reuse, or tensor parallel communication becomes important. It explains why weight compression has its cleanest speed story at low batch size, while low-precision GEMM matters increasingly as batch grows.

A.5 The one-weight compensation step behind GPTQ

For one output row, write the change in weights as δ\delta δ and local loss as δ⊤Hδ/2\delta ^\top H\delta /2δ⊤Hδ/2. Force coordinate jjj to its rounded value, so δj=qj−wj\delta _j=q_j-w_jδj​=qj​−wj​, and minimize over the free coordinates. With the current free-coordinate inverse curvature C=H−1C=H^{-1}C=H−1, the minimizing update is:

δF=(qj−wj)CF,jCj,j,ΔL=(qj−wj)22Cj,j.\begin{aligned}\delta_F&=(q_j-w_j)\frac{C_{F,j}}{C_{j,j}},\\\Delta L&=\frac{(q_j-w_j)^2}{2C_{j,j}}.\end{aligned}δF​ΔL​=(qj​−wj​)Cj,j​CF,j​​,=2Cj,j​(qj​−wj​)2​.​

The sign of the update follows the defined error qj−wjq_j-w_jqj​−wj​. Correlated columns can absorb part of the forced error; the inverse-curvature diagonal also tells how costly this rounding is locally. In practice GPTQ damps HHH, processes columns in blocks, and quantizes every output row in a shared order. [2]

A.6 Why AWQ's scaling has an optimum

Suppose an important input channel jjj is scaled by sj>1s_j>1sj​>1. If quantizing its scaled weights makes an error εj′\varepsilon'_jεj′​, its original-domain output contribution is approximately Xjεj′sj\frac{X_j\varepsilon'_j}{s_j}sj​Xj​εj′​​. That suggests larger sjs_jsj​ helps. But group-wise quantization recomputes the shared step from the scaled weights: a larger extreme can coarsen rounding for other channels. The first effect improves salient-channel error; the second can worsen the rest. AWQ's search over α\alpha α resolves that trade with calibration output error rather than assuming unlimited scaling helps. [3]

BGlossary

ActivationAn intermediate tensor produced for the current input; unlike weights, its range changes with requests.
Affine quantizationUniform integer grid with a scale and possibly a nonzero zero point.
CalibrationUsing representative inputs to choose scales, clipping thresholds, or reconstruction parameters.
DequantizationMapping stored low-bit codes back to approximate real values, often fused into a compute kernel.
Effective bits/weightTotal encoded weight storage divided by number of weights, including scale/zero metadata and exceptions.
E8M0Eight-bit exponent-only scale used by OCP MX recipes; it encodes powers of two, with no mantissa.
GEMMGeneral matrix multiplication; large GEMMs favor high arithmetic throughput.
GGUFModel file container used by llama.cpp; individual tensors inside can have different ggml numeric encodings.
GQAGrouped-query attention; several query heads share a smaller number of K/V heads, reducing cache size.
Group sizeNumber of values sharing quantization parameters such as a scale.
Hessian proxyHere, an input-correlation matrix such as 2X⊤X2X^\top X2X⊤X that estimates how layer-output error grows when weights change.
KV cacheStored attention keys and values from prior tokens for reuse during autoregressive decode.
KV residual windowRecent cached tokens retained at higher precision while older tokens are quantized.
NF4NormalFloat four-bit nonuniform codebook introduced in QLoRA for weights with roughly normal distributions.
MXFP4 / NVFP4Both use E2M1 four-bit values; MXFP4 has an E8M0 scale per 32, while NVFP4 uses an E4M3 scale per 16 and a tensor-level FP32 scale.
Orthogonal rotationA change of coordinates with RR⊤=IRR^\top =IRR⊤=I; paired transforms preserve the original floating-point computation.
OutlierA value or feature dimension whose magnitude makes a shared low-bit range inefficient.
PTQ / QATPost-training quantization / quantization-aware training.
RTNRound to nearest representable value, after choosing a grid.
Scale / zero pointParameters mapping between low-bit codes and approximate real values.
TTFT / TPOTTime to first token / time per output token.
Vector codebookA table whose index represents several weight values jointly instead of one scalar value.
W4A16Four-bit weights and 16-bit activations; says nothing by itself about scales or compute kernel.

CCheck yourself

1. Why can one extreme value make a four-bit group inaccurate?

It enlarges the shared scale. The distance between adjacent representable values grows, so ordinary small values are rounded more coarsely or to zero. Smaller groups, clipping, or a separate outlier path can help. §1.

2. What is the difference between GPTQ and W4A16?

GPTQ is a post-training algorithm that chooses/corrects quantized weights using calibration activations. W4A16 states stored weight and activation precision. GPTQ may produce a W4A16 checkpoint, but the labels answer different questions. §3–§4.

3. Why is an 8-bit W8A8 model sometimes faster than a 4-bit W4A16 model?

At large batch or in prefill, a native 8-bit GEMM may exploit low-precision arithmetic on both operands. W4A16 saves more weight bytes but may need dequantization and 16-bit compute. The answer depends on hardware and kernel. §0, §6.

4. A 7B model's weights fit comfortably after quantization, but 8K-context requests still cause OOM. Why?

KV cache scales with layers, K/V heads, head size, context length, and concurrent sequences. Weight quantization leaves it unchanged. In the worked 32-layer example, BF16 KV alone is 1 GiB per 8K sequence. §5.

5. Does smaller quantization error for weights guarantee better generated answers?

No. Output error is weighted by actual activations, and errors propagate through nonlinear layers and autoregressive token choices. Check held-out language modeling and target tasks, especially long-context and rare failures. §2, §7, §A.1.

6. Why can SmoothQuant change quantization difficulty without changing the original floating-point function?

It inserts a diagonal transform and its inverse: XW=(XD−1)(DW)XW=(XD^{-1})(DW)XW=(XD−1)(DW). This changes operand ranges before rounding while leaving their exact product unchanged. §3.2, §A.2.

7. What does “four bits per weight” omit in a capacity estimate?

Scale and zero-point metadata, higher-precision exceptions, alignment, tensors left unquantized, runtime buffers, and KV cache. §1.2, §4, §A.3.

8. What evidence would justify using two-bit KV cache?

Measurements on the exact model, backend, context lengths, concurrency, and tasks of interest, including long-context retrieval and generation. The KIVI result is a method result under its own evaluated settings, not an automatic guarantee. §5, §7.

9. GPTQ and AWQ both make four-bit weights. What changes inside each method?

GPTQ rounds a column and adjusts unrounded columns using calibration-input correlations. AWQ scales weights in salient input channels before rounding and applies the inverse scale to inputs. The first compensates error; the second reallocates quantization resolution. §3.5, §A.5–A.6.

10. Why does KIVI quantize keys per channel but values per token?

In its observed caches, persistent outlier dimensions make per-channel key groups reduce attention-score error. Values enter a sparse probability-weighted sum, so per-token grouping better protects each important token's value vector. The recent FP16 window helps hard generation tasks. §5.1, §9.5.

11. In §9.3, is AQLM always better than QuIP# at about two bits?

No. In the cited Llama-2-7B comparison AQLM leads before end-to-end tuning, while after both are tuned their results are close and QuIP# has slightly higher mean task accuracy. The comparison says nothing by itself about conversion time, kernel availability, or other models. §9.3.

12. Why can a close WikiText-2 perplexity miss a serious deployment regression?

It averages token prediction on one short-text distribution. Long context, non-English inputs, math/code tasks, and rare failures can respond differently. A multi-model long-context study found some much larger four-bit losses, so evaluate the intended workload directly. §7, §9.4.

13. What is the actual bit cost of FP8 values with one FP16 scale per 128?

For complete groups it is 8+16/128=8.1258+16/128=8.1258+16/128=8.125 bits/value. For arbitrary NNN, count N+2⌈N128⌉N+2\left\lceil\frac N{128}\right\rceilN+2⌈128N​⌉ bytes and divide by NNN. §4.2.

14. Do MXFP4, NVFP4, and GGUF Q4_K each use four bits per stored weight?

No. A full MXFP4 block uses 4.25 bits/value; NVFP4's basic 1D scheme approaches 4.5 bits/value plus one FP32 global scale per tensor; a Q4_K tensor uses 4.5 bits/value. A Q4_K_M file is a mixture of tensor types. §4.4–4.5.

15. Does TF32 cut the checkpoint to roughly 19 bits per weight?

No. TF32 changes the precision used by a compute path; its values still occupy 32 bits in storage. §4.1.
